entries.title: A2/A3 FP32 and INT8 matmul with a contiguous bias row
entries.surface: matmul(dst, a, b, m=, n=, k=, splitn=, splitk=, is_init=True, bias=) on A2/A3; Tensor(..., Position.L1, layout=Layout.ND) for the bias row; one kernel family across the a2 and a3 facades
study_for: `Layout.ND` on the bias tensor is what selects the A2 family's contiguous GM-to-L1 transfer. The operands are fractalized; the bias is a plain row, and saying so in the tensor declaration is how the staging is chosen. No padded A5-style transfer is substituted for it.

`is_init=True` is what makes split-K add the bias once. The `k=128` case runs eight passes, so a bias applied per pass would be eight times too large -- and because the values are exact, that failure is an exact multiple rather than a rounding difference. The failure output prints per-column deltas for the same reason: one delta per column points at the bias, a varying one at the product.

Split-N slices the bias row, and the two dtypes reach that differently. The INT32 bias already has the column addressing 32-element slices need; the FP32 bias gets there through an accepted same-width reinterpret to INT32 inside `matmul`, which keeps the addressing contiguous without converting any value. That asymmetry is the reason both dtypes have a split-N case.

The geometry constraints come from compact L1 storage with no implicit K padding: M a multiple of 16 in [16, 64], N one of 32/64/96, FP32 K a multiple of 16 and INT8 K a multiple of 32. The ten cases walk the minima, the maxima and a third N tile, so a path that only handled one tile or only even tile counts fails somewhere.

The bias is 3, 6, 9, ... -- distinct and increasing -- and `check_domain` asserts both. That is what makes a wrong N slice a wrong answer rather than the same one, and it is why the generator's choice of bias is part of the check rather than incidental.
do_not_copy_when: Your N is not 64 and you are using the no-split or split-K path. Both declare a static N=64 for the full bias row; only split-N takes an N argument.
You were going to convert the FP32 bias to INT32 to get column slicing. The reinterpret is at the same width and changes no value -- a conversion would change every one of them.

Your K is not aligned to its dtype's multiple. The L1 allocation here is compact, so there is no implicit padding to absorb a ragged K, and the guard refuses one rather than producing a plausible answer.
You need FP32 accumulation accuracy. Every operand is a dyadic eighth or a small integer, chosen so the product and the sum are exact. Nothing here generalises to real data.

entries.title: A2/A3 cube output transfers: a half round trip and an atomic add
entries.surface: an FP32 L0C tensor stored into an FP16 L1 tensor and fed back through matmul; the atomic_add() context manager around a fixpipe store; two destinations in one kernel, one accumulated and one plainly stored; OpExec(..., seed_outputs=True)
study_for: An L0C-to-L1 store can narrow, and that narrowing is a real rounding. `converted <<= product` writes the FP32 accumulator into an FP16 L1 tensor, which the second matmul then reads. The generator puts 2^-12 in the last column of `y` so the exact product carries fractions below an FP16 ULP -- and the reference refuses to run a case whose product would have survived the conversion unchanged, because then the example would prove nothing.

`atomic_add()` is a scoped mode, and whether it was restored is a separate question from whether it worked. The `seeded` case answers both: the accumulated destination arrives non-zero, so a lost initial value fails plane 0, and a second plain store to another non-zero destination fails plane 1 if the atomic mode leaked past its block.

The `overwrite` case is here for honesty as much as for coverage. The source it came from claimed in its header to retain a non-zero prior output; its body stored the product and then atomically added the same product, giving `2 * product`. That actual behaviour is what this case preserves, and it establishes nothing about seeding -- which is why the `seeded` case exists beside it rather than instead of it.

Seeding is a caller's responsibility. The destinations only arrive with their initial values because `OpExec` is constructed with `seed_outputs=True`, and each execution hands in fresh clones so an accumulating case cannot accumulate across runs. A direct caller that forgets the option gets a different kernel's worth of behaviour with no diagnostic.
do_not_copy_when: You are reading `overwrite_then_add` as evidence that a prior output survives. It does not test that. Its answer is twice the product, and the destination's initial value is irrelevant to it.
You are calling this kernel family without `seed_outputs=True`. The seeded case's arithmetic depends on the destination's contents; without seeding the result is whatever the launch left there.
You want FP16 accumulation. Nothing here accumulates in FP16 -- the accumulator is FP32 and only the *stored* intermediate is narrowed. That is a different operation from a half-precision matmul.
You need cross-core atomic accumulation. This is one cube participant. Two cores adding into the same GM bytes is a different synchronisation problem and no case here touches it.

entries.title: Three A2/A3 multiply-add precision paths into an initialized accumulator
entries.surface: muladddst(dst, a, b) accumulating into its destination, with adds(dst, c, 0.0) initializing it; the mixed path's repeat=, dst_blk_stride=, src1_blk_stride=, src2_blk_stride=, dst_rep_stride=, src1_rep_stride=, src2_rep_stride= form; four separate DBuff two-slot UB allocations; one kernel source across the a2 and a3 facades
study_for: `muladddst` accumulates into its destination. The destination is the accumulator, not a third operand, so `adds(acc, c, 0.0)` has to put `c` there first -- and `check_domain` refuses an input whose `c` is all zero, because then a kernel that skipped that step would agree anyway. Reading this as a three-operand FMA is the mistake the interface invites.

Four separate two-slot buffers, and the separation is the point. a, b and c are filled by MTE2; only the vector pipeline writes the accumulator. Mixing those roles onto one buffer is the defect this arrangement was reviewed to fix, and the 40,000-element case -- 157 tiles over two slots -- is what stops it from passing by luck.

The mixed path is in repeat mode, and the strides are per-dtype. `repeat = ceil(valid / 64)`, the FP32 destination steps 8 blocks per repeat and the FP16 sources step 4. Those numbers come from the element widths, not from the shapes, so they do not survive a dtype change. (Prose in the archive describing a count mode for this body is stale; the corrected body is the repeat form.)

The final repeat computes past the valid lanes on purpose, inside the fixed 5,120-element allocation, and only the logical prefix is published. `n65_tile64` has a second tile with one valid lane and 63 scratch lanes; `n5121_tile5120` is the largest allocation with the smallest second tile, which is where an overrun would land outside the buffer. A shared model calculation once checked a 5,184-element footprint for the valid 5,120-element tile; M10-036 repaired that.

The three bounds are per path and the reference is FP64. 1e-4 for the all-FP32 path and 2e-3 where the sources are FP16, each with a matching relative L2 bound so that a uniform bias cannot hide inside the element allowance. The dyadic cases make the arithmetic exact, so five of the ten cases do not depend on the budget at all.
do_not_copy_when: You want `dst = a * b`. Then the initialization is wrong and you need a plain multiply. `muladddst` always adds to what is there.

Your dtypes differ from these three pairs. The mixed path's repeat strides are derived from a 4-byte destination and 2-byte sources; another combination needs its own numbers, and getting them wrong computes the right values into the wrong lanes.
You are reading the 2e-3 bound as FP16 accuracy. It is the bound these inputs need in this operation order, over values in [-2, 2]. It is not a general statement about half precision.

Your allocation is sized to the valid length. The final repeat writes scratch lanes up to the next multiple of 64, so the buffer has to have them. Here they are always inside the 5,120-element allocation, and two cases exist to keep that true.

entries.title: A2/A3 element and 32-byte block gathers, by byte offset
entries.surface: gather(dst, src, offsets, repeat=, dst_rep_stride=) and gather_block(dst, src, offsets, repeat=, dst_blk_stride=, dst_rep_stride=), both taking a uint32 tensor of byte offsets; one kernel source across the a2 and a3 facades
study_for: The offsets are bytes, and this is where A2/A3 differs from A5. A5's register gather takes indices; these two helpers take byte offsets, so an offset of 4 selects the second FP32 rather than the fifth. A port between the two devices that carried the index arithmetic across produces a plausible, wrong gather -- and no diagnostic.

Element and block gather differ in how many offsets they read and how much each one brings. `gather` reads all 64 lanes and takes one FP32 from each; `gather_block` reads the first eight and takes a whole 32-byte block -- eight FP32 -- from each. In block mode the other 56 lanes are not addresses, and `check_domain` deliberately does not validate them, because treating them as addresses is itself a misreading.

The host owns the bounds check. The instruction will happily read a misaligned or out-of-range address, so the alignment and the in-bounds condition are asserted before the launch, per mode with that mode's own alignment. Both case families include the first and last legal address (0 and 508, 0 and 480) so the boundary is exercised rather than avoided.

The source is a permutation of 1000..1127, which makes every failure legible: a gathered value names the position it came from, and the failure output prints that position. Repeated offsets among the random ones are deliberate too -- a gather that deduplicated, or that wrote each destination lane once regardless, would disagree.
do_not_copy_when: You are porting from or to A5. The contract is different: indices there, byte offsets here. Nothing about this example transfers except the shape of the problem.

You are filling all 64 offset lanes for a block gather. Eight are read. Populating the rest is work discarded, and expecting the rest to be gathered is a misreading of the instruction, not a defect in it.
You are relying on the instruction to reject a bad address. It does not. The check here is in the host, before the launch, and it is not optional.

entries.title: Signed-INT4 cube products with a logical K shorter than the carrier
entries.surface: INT32 GM carriers holding eight low-first signed nibbles with the logical K as a separate scalar; a device-side normalization pass using scalar loads and stores into private GM scratch plus a scalar data cache clean before MTE2; two K-chunk L1 allocations and is_init=(k0 == 0) accumulation on A2/A3
study_for: The logical length and the physical storage are separate arguments, deliberately. The carriers are INT32 with eight low-first signed nibbles; `K` is a scalar. So `K=9` is two carriers with fifteen nibbles of padding, and the padding is generated data -- not zeros, and not the caller's problem to zero.

C220's INT4 MMAD consumes both nibbles of the final byte even when the logical K is odd (M10-099), so the kernel normalizes on the device. One cube launch copies each carrier into a private GM scratch argument, clears the unused high nibbles of the last word with scalar stores, and cleans the scalar data cache before MTE2 -- that last step because the device just wrote those bytes with the scalar unit and MTE2 is about to read them. The caller's tensors are untouched, and `execute` asserts that.

`source137` and `source137_pad15` are the same logical input with different padding nibbles, and their outputs must be bit-identical. That pair is the only thing in the matrix that checks the normalization at all: every other case would pass just as well with the padding contributing, because its own reference would then be wrong in the same way -- except it would not, since the reference decodes only the logical prefix.

There are two K-chunk allocations, and the boundary is a case. A chunk of more than 64 logical values uses the main 16-carrier L1 allocation; at most 64 uses a separate 8-carrier one. `k64` and `k65` sit on either side of that branch, so a kernel that used one path for both fails one of them.

The reference decodes nibbles with integer masks and shifts and multiplies in INT64. It calls no int4 packer, no decoder, no execution codec and no kernel helper -- which is what makes the sixteen signed values in the `k64` payload a real check of the sign extension rather than a comparison of the library against itself.
do_not_copy_when: You are assuming padding nibbles are ignored by the hardware. They are not; the final byte is consumed whole. Either normalize them, as this kernel does on the device, or make the caller guarantee them -- but do not assume.
You are skipping the scalar data cache clean. The normalization writes through the scalar unit and MTE2 reads those bytes next; without the clean the transfer can read what was there before.
Your carrier is not INT32 low-first. No other carrier type is accepted here, and the nibble order is part of the public contract rather than an implementation choice.
Your K exceeds 257 or your M/N exceed 129. Those are the declared bounds; the tiling and the two allocations are sized for them.

entries.title: A2/A3 manual masks, a counted tail, and what the count restores
entries.surface: set_mask(low, high) and reset_mask() at kernel scope; adds / muls / dup with repeat= against the same operations with count=; one kernel source across the a2 and a3 facades
study_for: A counted operation returns to the normal mask, not to the manual one. `set_mask(0, 7)` activates three lanes; the counted `muls(..., count=70)` overrides that for seventy; and the uncounted `adds(..., repeat=2)` that follows covers all 128. If the count had saved and restored the manual mask, the third output would hold its initialization from lane 3 onwards -- which is exactly what the third output exists to rule out, and what `check_domain` asserts cannot be mistaken for a pass.

Inactive lanes keep what the destination already held. The two masked outputs are pre-filled with `dup(-9.0)` and `dup(-7.0)` and those fills are compared, so the example distinguishes a lane the operation wrote from a lane a mask kept inactive. The third destination is deliberately *not* filled: nothing `dup`s it, so a lane the uncounted operation did not write reads back as the NaN poison -- which is what a restored manual mask looks like, and why a sentinel value would not have worked there (x + 1 can legitimately be -9.0).

Two ways to bound a vector operation, side by side. `repeat` counts whole 64-lane vectors and respects the mask; `count` names a lane count and overrides it. Both appear in one body over one input, which is the cheapest way to see that they are not two spellings of the same thing.

Integer-valued inputs and sentinel fills are what make the comparison bitwise. `x + 3`, `2 * x` and `x + 1` over integers in [-100, 100] are exact in FP32, so there is nothing for a tolerance to absorb and the fills are unambiguous.
do_not_copy_when: You expect your manual mask to survive a counted operation. It does not. Set it again after the count, or do not rely on it.
You expect inactive lanes to be zero. They hold whatever the destination held. Initialize it, as this kernel does with `dup`, or accept an undefined tail.
You are on A5. The mask vocabulary there is `MaskReg` and per-operation mask operands, not `set_mask` / `reset_mask` state. This example's whole subject is the A2/A3 form.

entries.title: A2/A3 row reduction in two stages, broadcast back in two more
entries.surface: cadd(dst, src, repeat=, src_blk_stride=, src_rep_stride=, count_per_rep=) in two stages; brcb(dst, src, repeat=, dst_blk_stride=, dst_rep_stride=) twice to fill 64 lanes from one value; dup initializing every scratch buffer; one kernel source across the a2 and a3 facades
study_for: `cadd`'s two strides count different units. The destination repeat stride counts result *elements*; the source repeat stride counts 32-byte *blocks*. That asymmetry is the single easiest thing to get wrong in this call, and the `width_128` and `width_256` cases are where a confusion between them produces a wrong sum rather than a coincidence.

Reducing a row wider than a vector takes two stages with different counts. The first `cadd` reads 64 lanes per repeat and leaves one partial per group; the second reduces `groups` partials, and its `count_per_rep` is that live count -- not 64. The scratch is a full 64-lane allocation that `dup` zeroes first, so reading too many lanes would be harmless here; that is a safety property of the initialization, not something the cases can catch.

Broadcasting one runtime value to 64 lanes takes two `brcb` calls, because one fills a 32-byte block. The first turns the total into eight copies inside one block; the second takes those eight and fills all 64 lanes of the scale. A single call would leave 56 lanes at whatever they held -- zero here, which would silently zero seven eighths of the product.

The scale is computed on the device, not passed in. That is what makes this a broadcast example rather than a scaling one: the multiplier is the row's own sum, produced by the reduction two stages earlier, and every group of the output multiplies against the same 64-lane scale.

Small integer inputs make the sums and the products exact in FP32, so the comparison is bitwise. That is a property of these inputs. This example sets no reduction tolerance for arbitrary floating data, and a reduction over real values has an order-dependent answer that none of this addresses.
do_not_copy_when: You are copying the stride arguments without their units. Elements for the destination, blocks for the source. The numbers look interchangeable and are not.

Your row is not a multiple of 64. Every width here is, so the first reduction stage has no partial group and the second has no partial count. A ragged row needs a masked or counted final repeat, which this example does not have.
You expect one `brcb` to fill a vector. It fills a block. The two-call form here is the shape of that limitation.

Your values are arbitrary floats. Then the sum's order matters and the comparison has to be a tolerance -- and the reference has to mirror the kernel's reduction order, which this one does not attempt because it does not need to.

entries.title: A counted vector tail, and a packed compare mask driving a select, on A2 and A3
entries.surface: muls and add with an explicit count= over a larger allocation; compare(predicate, x, y, CompareMode.GT) into a packed DT.uint8 mask tile; select(..., SelectMode.TENSOR_TENSOR, tmp_addr_buf=) with a DT.uint32 scratch address buffer; a dynamic GM shape symbol; kernel(mode="vec") from the a2 or a3 facade
study_for: `count=` is how a vector instruction is told its logical extent, which is not its allocation. The tile holds 128 lanes and 70 are live; the other 58 are allocated and transferred and never computed. 70 is chosen because it is neither a full tile nor a round fraction of one -- `check_domain` refuses a count that divides the capacity, since such a case could pass with the count ignored.

The predicate is *packed*: one bit per lane, so 64 lanes of comparison result live in a `DT.uint8[1, 32]` tile rather than in 64 bytes. That is the layout `compare` produces and `select` consumes, and reading it as one byte per lane is the mistake the shape makes visible.
`select` takes a scratch address buffer, `tmp_addr_buf`, which is a real allocation the caller owns rather than something the instruction finds for itself.

The answer for the select case is an element-wise maximum, and `check_domain` requires both sides to be chosen somewhere in the case. A mask read in the wrong direction is then wrong in about half the lanes instead of in none, and a select that always took one operand fails immediately.
The facade is an argument: `kernels(device)` decorates the same bodies with A2's or A3's `kernel`, so this source is both devices' example and `--device` runs it as each.
do_not_copy_when: You expect the lanes past `count=` to be defined. They are not written; here they are not even published, because the output is exactly the logical extent.
You are treating the predicate as one byte per lane. It is one bit per lane, and the tile shape says so.
You want `select` without a scratch address buffer. It needs one, and it is the caller's allocation.
Your device is not A2 or A3. The facade is checked; a different profile has its own vector vocabulary and its own mask layout rules.

entries.title: The smallest complete vector kernel: load, scale, add, store
entries.surface: kernel(mode="vec") and a bare @vf decorator; Tensor(DT.float, [1, 64], Position.UB) staging; Reg(DT.float) loads with <<=, muls against a Python float and add of two registers; auto_sync() around the transfers; OpExec with an explicit timeout, and Kernel.name / .device / .mode / .ir through --inspect
study_for: The shortest path from a Python function to something that runs: three instructions in the `@vf`, one `auto_sync()` block moving the rows in and the result out, one launch. Read this one first.

The bitwise comparison is earned rather than lucky. A multiply by two is exact in FP32 and the add is a single rounding, so the host's `2 * x + y` performs exactly the two operations the register performs, in the same order. `check_domain` asserts the doubling is exact instead of assuming it.

`mixed_magnitudes` gives each lane its own binary exponent, from 2**-32 to 2**31, with the two operands' scales running opposite ways. It still agrees bit for bit -- which is the point, because it says the exactness belongs to the operations and not to the operands being small.

`--inspect` prints what the frontend made of the kernel -- its name, device, mode, the IR dialect and the count of located operations -- and writes the surface IR. Nothing is compiled or run, so it is the cheapest way to see that a kernel parsed and where each operation came from.

The one launcher and backend pairing that cannot work is checked here: the `pypto` launcher runs the sources only the `pypto_pro` backend prints. The runtime accepts any pairing, so this example refuses that one itself, at the argument parser.
do_not_copy_when: You need more than one row or more than one core. Everything here is [1, 64] on one vector core; a real tiling has ownership questions this example does not raise.
Your arithmetic is not exact. Two operations with one rounding is what allows the byte comparison; anything else needs a tolerance and a reference that states it.
You are treating `--inspect` as evidence that the kernel works. It shows what the frontend built, nothing more -- no lowering, no source emission, no execution.

entries.title: Implementing the public Backend protocol and publishing it as an entry point
entries.surface: ascriptor.backends.base.Backend, Capabilities, ResourceLimits and Artifacts implemented by a class outside the library; discover() and get() over the ascriptor.backends entry-point group; compile_kernel(..., backend="<registered name>"); a pyproject.toml declaring that entry point
study_for: What a backend has to provide, as a list you can run: an instance of `Backend` returning `Capabilities`, `ResourceLimits` for a device, and `Artifacts` from a lowered module. Each is checked and reported on its own line, so 'it implements the protocol' is six verdicts rather than one claim.

The adapter is transparent on purpose. It delegates every instruction to CCE and its emitted files and entry symbol are compared byte for byte against CCE's own -- so what the example demonstrates is the *protocol*, with the lowering held fixed. A backend that actually lowered differently would need its own semantic and vendor compilation gates, and nothing here would stand in for them.

The one thing the adapter adds is a `teaching_adapter` key in the artifact metadata, and that is checked too. It is the seam where a real backend would record what it did, and it is the only difference the artifact comparison is allowed to have.

Discovery is exercised the standard way -- `discover()` and `get()` over the `ascriptor.backends` entry-point group -- using temporary distribution metadata placed on this process's import path. Nothing is installed, no dependency is touched, and the directory is removed when the check ends. `pyproject.toml` is the file that shows what an installed distribution would publish, and `main.py` checks that it declares the same group, name and object path that the temporary metadata used. Otherwise the two could drift and the example would be demonstrating discovery of something nobody could install.

A conformance claim gets one numerical result behind it: the copy kernel runs through the *registered name* and its output is compared to the input bitwise. The kernel is a copy so that the backend is the only variable -- a difference is the backend's.
`check_domain` requires the reference not to alias the input. For a copy that matters: a kernel that handed back the caller's own tensor would compare equal for the wrong reason.
do_not_copy_when: You are adding an instruction rather than adapting one. This example establishes protocol conformance and discovery only; a new lowering needs its own numerical references, its own vendor compilation and its own hardware evidence.
You expect the capabilities or limits to be yours. They are CCE's, returned unchanged. A backend for different hardware has to answer those questions itself, and this example says nothing about how.

You are treating the temporary metadata as an installation. It exists for the duration of one check and is on this process's path only. Ship the `pyproject.toml` entry point if you want a backend others can discover.

You are reading a model run as backend execution. `sim` and `pipesim` run the library's own models; the backend's own compilation and execution are separate stages, and only the non-model launchers reach them.

entries.title: Block gather by byte offset, into 64-bit lanes
entries.surface: ub_to_reg_gatherb(dst, src_ub, index_reg) with 32-byte block granularity; reinterpret(tensor, DT.uint32) to read an INT32 index tensor as unsigned offsets; ub_to_reg_normal / reg_to_ub_normal around it
study_for: The offsets are bytes. This is the one thing to get right and the easiest to get wrong: an index lane holding 4 does not select the fifth int64, it selects a block four bytes in -- which is not even block-aligned. The host multiplies block numbers by 32, and `check_domain` refuses an offset that is unaligned or past the source, because the instruction itself will not.

Only the first eight index lanes are read. The index register is 64 lanes wide and 56 of them are zero here and ignored. That asymmetry between the register's width and the instruction's appetite is worth knowing before you build an index by broadcasting something.

The index is unsigned, and `reinterpret` is how it gets there. The tensor is declared INT32 because that is what the host fills; `reinterpret(idx_s, DT.uint32)` gives the same bytes an unsigned type for the gather to read. No conversion happens -- it is a type view, and mixing the two up would only matter for an offset large enough to look negative.

Both halves of every lane carry information. The source spans +/-2^40, so a gather that moved only the low 32 bits of each int64 fails; `check_domain` asserts that span rather than hoping for it. The poison, 0x1234567812345678, is chosen the same way: both of its halves are non-zero, so a lane nothing wrote cannot be confused for a gathered one.

Repeated offsets are legal. The `repeated_blocks` case selects block 15 and block 7 twice each, and the reference simply lists what each output block should be. That makes two separate mistakes visible -- an implementation that deduplicated its offsets, and one that wrote over a lane it had already filled.
do_not_copy_when: You want an element gather. This is a block gather: 32 bytes at a time, aligned. Selecting individual elements is a different instruction with a different index meaning, and nothing here exercises it.
Your block size is not 32 bytes. The granularity is the hardware's, not a parameter. Four int64, eight int32, sixteen int16 -- the count changes with the dtype but the 32 bytes do not.

You are filling all 64 index lanes and expecting all of them to matter. Eight are read. A build that populates the rest is doing work the instruction throws away, and one that populates fewer than eight leaves the first eight partly undefined.

entries.title: Two-slot rings in UB and GM, with the GM round trip ordered by hand
entries.surface: DBuff(f32, [1, 64], Position.UB) indexed by beat; GMBuff(f32, [1, 64], slots=2, per_core=False) as a GM workspace ring; SEvent(Pipe.MTE3, Pipe.MTE2) set and waited inside auto_sync(); one kernel(mode="vec") launch
study_for: What `auto_sync()` does and does not cover. It orders everything on chip, including the reuse of both UB rings. It does not order a round trip through GM, so the MTE3 write and the MTE2 read back are ordered by an explicit `SEvent(Pipe.MTE3, Pipe.MTE2)` -- naming exactly the two pipes involved.

Five beats over two slots, on purpose. The rings wrap twice and the fifth beat takes slot 0 for the third time, so a kernel that reused a slot still in flight has an opportunity to do so. A four-beat version would not reach that third reuse.

A `GMBuff` with `per_core=False` is one workspace shared by the launch rather than one per core. With a single vector core that distinction changes nothing here, which is exactly why it is worth reading before copying into a kernel where there are several.

The answer is a copy, which is the point: any ordering mistake shows up as a whole row in the wrong place rather than as a small numeric difference. The rows are ten apart by construction, `check_domain` asserts that separation, and `compare` reports which source row each wrong row actually came from.
do_not_copy_when: You have more than one core and a shared GM workspace. `per_core=False` means one ring for the launch; with several cores writing it, the ownership question this example never asks becomes the whole problem.
You are relying on autosync for a GM round trip. It does not order one. The event here is not decoration.
Your slot count divides your beat count evenly. Then no slot is ever reused while another is in flight in the way the fifth beat does here, and the reuse this example is about is not being exercised.

entries.title: Defined-lane 64-bit casts, and packed INT4 both ways
entries.surface: cast(dst, src, CastConfig(round_mode=, saturate=, reg_layout=RegLayout.ZERO), mask); Reg(DT.int4) with reinterpret(DT.uint8) and pack4(); ub_to_reg_unpack4; reg_to_ub_normal through a MaskType.LOWEST32 mask
study_for: A single-register 64-bit cast defines half of what you might expect. Widening i32 to i64 doubles the bytes per lane, so one destination register holds 32 lanes and source lanes 32..63 have nowhere to go; narrowing i64 to i32 fills only the first 32 destination lanes for the same reason. Both stores go through a `MaskType.LOWEST32` mask, which is what stops the second source register -- undefined here -- from being read. Publishing the full 64 lanes would produce plausible garbage in the upper half rather than an error.

The argument-free i64-to-i32 narrowing ignores CTRL. It discards high bits whatever the saturation flags say (D-233), which makes it a different operation from a saturating narrowing rather than a special case of one. The inputs include +/-268435472 so the discarded word is visible in the result.

`i64` to `f32` rounds toward zero, and stating that took work on the reference side. Torch's own conversion rounds to nearest, so the reference computes the nearest result and then steps it back toward zero with `nextafter` when its magnitude overshot the integer. Without that, the reference would disagree with the kernel on exactly the values past FP32's exact range -- which is where the inputs are.

INT4 packs four nibbles to a byte with the low nibble carrying the even lane. `pack4()` on a `uint8` reinterpretation of an int4 register produces the dense carriers; `ub_to_reg_unpack4` reverses it, spreading 64 dense bytes into one byte in every four. The `i4_widen` carriers include 0x8F and 0x70 -- a negative nibble beside a positive one in the same byte -- so a widening that read the nibbles in the wrong order disagrees everywhere rather than subtly.

The reference never routes an integer through floating point. It packs signed nibbles directly with `clamp(-8, 7) & 15`, and narrows with Python-level ties-to-even, so the reference's own rounding is not borrowing the behaviour it is supposed to be checking.
do_not_copy_when: You need all 64 lanes of a 64-bit cast. That needs two destination registers and a second store; the forms here define 32, and the mask on the store is what keeps the promise honest.

Your values are not finite, or your conversion can overflow. The declared domain is finite values with int64 magnitudes below 2^40 and float-to-int64 inputs strictly inside the type. NaN handling and overflow are not claimed here -- `cast_saturation` is where the boundary behaviour is checked.
Your INT4 range is not [-8, 7]. The saturating narrowings clamp there, and an unsigned or offset nibble encoding is a different packing with a different reference.
You are assuming the narrowing respects your saturation setting. The argument-free i64-to-i32 form does not, on purpose. A saturating narrowing is a different call.

entries.title: Four CTRL saturation modes against a per-instruction CastConfig
entries.surface: get_saturation_flag / set_saturation_flag for "global" and "cast" as raw CTRL bits; CastConfig(saturate=, round_mode=RoundMode.TO_EVEN, reg_layout=RegLayout.ZERO); barrier(Pipe.ALL) before every mode change; unroll(4) over the CTRL pairs
study_for: The two flags are raw bits and their meaning is not symmetric. `global=0` defers to whatever the instruction's `CastConfig(saturate=...)` said; `global=1, cast=0` forces saturation and `global=1, cast=1` forces wrapping, both overriding the instruction. So the per-instruction setting is a request, not a decision, and three of the four modes do something the CastConfig did not ask for. The reference states the same rule in one line -- `mode == 2 or (mode < 2 and register even)` -- which is worth comparing against the prose.

Each case walks all four modes in one launch, so the output is a matrix rather than four runs. Row `m`, 128-lane block `r` is what mode `m` did to conversion `r`, where the four conversions are integer-with-saturate, integer-without, then the same two for float. Reading a column tells you which modes changed that conversion's behaviour; reading a row tells you which conversions that mode affected.

`RegLayout.ZERO` defines the odd lanes as zero, and they are compared. That is not padding to ignore: the layout is part of what the cast does, and a run whose odd lanes carried leftover data would be a different result even with every even lane right.

Two input families for the same matrix. The `ties` family sits on +/-0.5 boundaries and the integer type's edges (-32769, -32768, 32767, 32768), where ties-to-even and modular wrapping are each decided; the `specials` family is +/-inf, NaN, +/-2^40 and -32768.0 exactly, where saturation has to answer the type's limits and the NaN has to answer zero. Neither family alone covers both behaviours.

Three levels of state again, and a barrier at every change. The launch's pair is saved first, the case's `initial_mode` pair installed and saved, the four working pairs walked, the case's pair restored and checked into row 4, and the launch's pair put back last. `barrier(Pipe.ALL)` precedes each change because CTRL is shared by the pipes -- work still in flight would see an unpredictable mixture.
do_not_copy_when: You are relying on CastConfig(saturate=True) to saturate. It does when `global=0`, and it does not when `global=1, cast=1`. If the surrounding code can change CTRL, the instruction's own setting is not the answer.

You expect a NaN to propagate through a narrowing cast. It does not here -- a saturating conversion of NaN is zero, which the reference states explicitly. That is a property of the conversion, not a defect.

You are leaving CTRL where your kernel left it. This example restores two levels and publishes proof of one of them; a kernel that does not is a kernel whose successor's casts behave differently for reasons nobody will find quickly.
You want the saturation behaviour of a widening cast. Every conversion here narrows to int16. A widening cast has no value to clamp and the flags mean nothing to it.

entries.title: Eight complex register operations at both physical widths
entries.surface: Reg(DT.complex64) and Reg(DT.complex32) with add / sub / mul / div, adds / muls against a Python complex literal, abs into a real register of the matching width, and dup of a literal; GM[DT.complex64] and GM[DT.complex32] carriers; eight separate kernel(mode="vec") entries
study_for: Sixteen named outputs, not one. Eight operations at two widths each get their own destination, their own comparison and their own bound, so an operation that was never emitted fails as itself instead of disappearing into an average over a combined result. That is the whole reason there are eight kernels rather than two.

Complex results are compared as FP32 real/imaginary planes, via `torch.view_as_real(value.to(torch.complex64))`. NumPy cannot represent Torch's `complex32`, so on some hosts the imaginary component of a half-precision complex result is not observable at all; as planes it always is, and a multiply that dropped the cross term cannot hide in the half that was never read.

The bounds differ between the widths by a factor of twenty -- 0.0003 for `complex64`, 0.006 for `complex32` -- because `complex32`'s components are FP16. Each output also carries a relative-L2 bound at the same number, which an element bound alone would not catch if a whole row drifted.

The abs kernels allocate a full 256-byte UB tile, `Tensor(DT.float, [1, 2 * C64_COLS], ...)`, and publish only the defined first half with `ub_abs[0:1, 0:C64_COLS]`. The physical store spans the whole 256 bytes; the defined lanes are the first half. Sizing the allocation to the logical output is the mistake this shape exists to prevent.

The reference expands the arithmetic itself in complex128 -- `mul` as `(ar*br - ai*bi, ar*bi + ai*br)`, `div` over `br*br + bi*bi` -- and calls no DSL complex helper and no execution codec. That is what makes the literal case's Pythagorean values, where abs is exactly 5, a check of the device rather than a comparison of the library against itself.

`zero_numerator` is in the matrix because it is where a control stops working. With `a` zeroed, multiply, divide, absolute value and scalar multiply are all legitimately zero, so replacing those outputs with zeros proves nothing there -- only corruption and shape do. The other three cases are what cover them.
do_not_copy_when: Your denominator can approach zero. The domain here is `0.125 <= |b| <= 12`, deliberately conditioned; no singular or non-finite complex division is claimed or checked.
You are comparing complex tensors as complex. Convert to real planes first, or the imaginary half of a `complex32` result may not be compared at all on your host.
You are carrying one bound across both widths. FP16 components need twenty times the room FP32 components do, and a single bound is either too loose for one width or too tight for the other.
Your operands leave the bounded domain. Inputs are finite with `|a| <= 8`; infinities and NaNs are outside this example and nothing here establishes how they propagate through these registers.
You are sizing an abs staging tile to its logical width. The store is 256 bytes wide regardless; publish a slice of a full tile rather than allocating a half one.

entries.title: A cube bias across no split, split-N and split-K
entries.surface: matmul(dst, a, b, m=, n=, k=, splitn=, splitk=, bias=) with the bias as a contiguous L1 row; gm_to_l1_pad staging that row; Position.L1 and Position.L0C tensors in a kernel(mode="cube") launch
study_for: The three staging modes are `matmul` parameters, not three kernels. `splitn=32` and `splitk=16` change how the same call partitions work inside one core, and the body around them is identical. Reading the three cases together is reading what those two keywords do.

Where the bias belongs in a split-K accumulation: on the init tile, once. The K dimension is accumulated in two passes here, and a bias added on both of them doubles exactly -- which is why the bias values are exact in FP32 and the comparison is bitwise. With a tolerance, or with a bias of zero, that failure would be invisible.

Each property of the bias row buys one detectable mistake, and `check_domain` asserts all three. Non-zero catches a bias never applied -- except in column 31, where `(arange(64) - 31) / 4` crosses zero and that one column can detect nothing; the assertion allows exactly one such column and refuses a second. Non-uniform -- `(arange(64) - 31) / 4`, sixty-four distinct values -- catches a split-N half that took the wrong slice of the row. Multiples of a quarter keep every value exact in FP32 so the comparison can be over bits.

The bias is a contiguous L1 row, moved with `gm_to_l1_pad`, and not ND2NZ-fractalized like the operands. That asymmetry in how the three L1 tensors are staged is part of the interface rather than an implementation detail of this example.

The reference does not know which split ran. It is one matmul plus one bias addition, so the three cases are three independent paths being held to a single statement of what the answer is -- rather than three references that could each drift toward their own kernel.
do_not_copy_when: You are looking for FP32 or HF32 accuracy behaviour. The inputs are small integers in [-3, 3] and the bias is a multiple of a quarter, chosen so that everything is exact. Nothing here generalises to accumulation error on real data.

Your bias is per-row rather than per-column. This is a [1, N] row broadcast down the output's rows -- the usual shape for a matmul bias. A per-row bias is a different broadcast and a different staging.

You are writing the split loops yourself. `splitn` and `splitk` are shortcuts; a hand-written tiling has to place the bias on its own init tile, and that is precisely the mistake the `splitk` case here exists to catch.

entries.title: A convolution output tile, with its physical raster tail
entries.surface: conv2d(dst, feature_map, weights, Conv2D(kh, kw, stride=, dilation=, pad=), h=, w=, c=, cout=, m0=, tile_k=) with an NC1HWC0 feature map in L1 and [Cout_p, K] row-major weights
study_for: The physical tile is 16 rows and the logical output may be fewer, and the difference is not padding. `load3d` continues producing raster windows past Ho*Wo (D-223), and those rows hold real convolution results. The `stride_tail` case has four logical rows and twelve tail rows, and all sixteen are compared -- a consumer of the logical convolution takes the first `output_rows` and leaves the rest alone.

How the reference reaches the tail without becoming a second implementation. It never decodes simulator storage and never reproduces the load3d loop: it extends the *bottom* zero pad of the original image until an ordinary `conv2d` produces exactly those extra windows. So the tail is stated in convolution arithmetic, which is the only way it can be an independent check rather than a transcription.

The packing is the host's job, and `check_domain` verifies it. An NC1HWC0 feature map with C1=1 and C0=16 zero-pads three real channels to sixteen; the weights are [Cout_p, K] with K = kh*kw*c0 = 144, five real filters zero-padded to sixteen. Both paddings are asserted zero, and so are the reference's output columns past Cout=5 -- a non-zero carrier would make the product wrong in a way the shapes cannot show.

Three geometries, and each one moves a different thing. `same_padding` fills the tile with logical output. `stride_tail` is where the physical tail exists at all. `dilation` widens the 3x3 kernel to span five input positions, so every window touches the padding -- and an implementation that applied the dilation to the padding instead of to the kernel would still produce a 4x4 output, which is why the values are compared and not just the shape.

Small integer FP16 inputs are what make the comparison bitwise. The convolution accumulates in FP32 and every product and sum is exact, so there is nothing for a tolerance to absorb -- and nothing this unit claims about FP16 accumulation error on real data.
do_not_copy_when: You are treating all 16 rows as your output. Only the first `output_rows` are the logical convolution; the rest are the hardware's raster continuation and belong to nobody.
You expect the packing to happen for you. NC1HWC0 and the [Cout_p, K] weight order are the host's responsibility here, and the zero carrier channels are what makes a partly filled tile meaningful.

Your geometry is not one of the three. `make_conv` refuses anything else on purpose -- the reference's bottom-pad arithmetic is derived for these, and a fourth geometry needs that derivation redone rather than the guard relaxed.
You are after convolution accuracy in FP16. Every value here is a small integer chosen so the FP32 result is exact. Accumulation error is a different subject.

entries.title: The smallest complete cube tile, on all four device facades
entries.surface: matmul(accumulator, lhs, rhs) with NZ L1 operands and an L0C accumulator stored into a complete ND GM matrix; kernel(mode="cube") obtained from importlib.import_module("ascriptor." + device), so the same body serves a2, a3, a5 and a5pr
study_for: The shortest cube kernel: two L1 operands, one L0C accumulator, one `matmul`, one store. M = N = K = 16, the smallest complete tile, so no tiling, no split and no tail is in the way of reading it.

The facade is a factory argument. `make_kernel(device)` imports `ascriptor.<device>` and decorates the same body with that facade's `kernel`, so this text is the A2, A3, A5 and A5PR kernel and `--device` runs it as each. A kernel this simple is portable across the four; one that touched a device-specific instruction would not be, and that is worth knowing before copying.

The bitwise comparison is earned. Integer operands in [-4, 4] with K = 16 make every sum at most 4096, well inside FP32's exact-integer range, and `check_domain` asserts both the bound and that every result is integral. Widen the operands and the assertion fails rather than the comparison quietly becoming wrong.

The operands go to L1 as NZ tiles while the destination is complete ND. Two layouts in four lines, which is the smallest place to see that the cube's operand layout and its result layout are separate questions.
do_not_copy_when: Your tile is not complete. There is no tail handling here at all; M, N and K are exactly 16.
Your operands are not exactly representable. The byte comparison rests on that; ordinary FP16 data needs a tolerance and a reference that states one.

You assume every kernel is portable across the facades because this one is. It is portable because it uses only what all four have. A device-specific instruction, a different L0 capacity or a different fixpipe rule breaks that immediately.

entries.title: MX products at three payload formats, two paths, nonuniform scales
entries.surface: matmul_mx(dst, a, b, scale_a, scale_b, m=, n=, k=) against l1_to_l0_mx + mmad_mx; gm_to_l1_mx_scale_nd2nz packing dense scale codes; Tensor.reinterpret to DT.fp4_e2m1 / DT.fp4_e1m2 / DT.e4m3 / DT.e5m2; the DT.mx_e4m3 and DT.mx_e5m2 compatibility aliases
study_for: The aliases do not attach scales. `DT.mx_e4m3` and `DT.mx_e5m2` name the same physical bytes as the ordinary FP8 storage types; what makes a product an MX product is the `l1_to_l0_mx` load and the `mmad_mx` / `matmul_mx` compute. Reading the alias as 'the MX type' is the misunderstanding this example is arranged to prevent -- and the alias form needs the M10-017 repair, while the reference is unchanged either way.

Two paths over one set of inputs. The shortcut is one call; the explicit path allocates L0A and L0B tensors, loads each operand with its scale through `l1_to_l0_mx`, and computes with `mmad_mx`. Every format runs both, and the pair agreeing is what establishes that the shortcut is the same operation rather than a similar one.

The scales are dense per row and per K32 group, and nonuniform in both directions on purpose -- `125 + (row + group) % 5` for one operand and a different combination for the other. A packing that transposed the two axes, or a compute that took group 0's scale for every group, produces a power-of-two error in a whole row or a whole 32-column band, which the failure output points at.

The reference decodes the payloads without the library. FP8 is arithmetic -- exponent field, fraction, bias, and the subnormal branch -- and FP4 is a lookup table per layout, with A as E2M1 and B as E1M2 in the mixed case. No ascriptor codec is imported, so the decode is genuinely independent of the thing being checked.

Why it can be bitwise. The payload pools are restricted exponent bands and the scale codes are 125..129, so every value is dyadic and the whole 128-element dot product lands exactly in FP32. Widen either and the comparison has to become a tolerance -- and then it stops being able to see a one-group scale error.
do_not_copy_when: You need a transposed or compact-tail MX tile. This example declares a fully aligned, untransposed K=128 tile and establishes nothing else: no transpose, no compact tail, no exceptional scale codes, and no FP8 mixed with FP4 in one product.
Your payloads span the whole format. The exponent bands here are chosen so the dot product is exact; arbitrary FP8 values need a tolerance and a different argument about what the comparison proves.

You expected the dtype to carry the scale. It does not. A kernel that loads an MX operand with an ordinary `l1_to_l0` and then calls `mmad_mx` has no scales attached, and nothing in the type system will say so.

entries.title: Five fixpipe requantization paths out of L0C
entries.surface: Tensor.requant(scale=, offset=) applied to an L0C accumulator on its way to GM; the input/accumulator/destination dtype triple selecting the conversion (f16/f32 and i8/i32 into i8, u8 or f16)
study_for: The dtype triple is what selects the conversion. There is no mode enumeration in the instruction: the input dtype, the accumulator dtype and the destination dtype together decide whether this is a quantization, a requantization or a dequantization. The five cases are five triples, and the kernel derives all three dtypes from the mode name so the mapping is in one place.

The order of operations is scale, round, offset, clamp -- and the offset is after the rounding, which is observable. The reference computes `(product * scale).round() + offset` then clamps, and the odd dot products land on exact halves so ties-to-even is decided before the offset moves them anywhere. An implementation that offset first would round different lanes.

The signed and unsigned destinations are the same path with a different clamp, which is why they are two cases with one seed apart. `fp32_i8` clamps to [-128, 127] and `fp32_u8` to [0, 255], so the planted -8 column merely rounds in one and is clamped to zero in the other. Either case alone leaves the destination's signedness untested.

The scales are 0.5 and 0.25 because those are exact in the hardware's float19 parameter field. That is a deliberate restriction: an arbitrary scale would put the parameter's own packing into the comparison, and this example has no independent reference for that packing. `check_domain` refuses anything else rather than letting one in quietly.

The saturation is reached, not assumed. Rows of the first operand and columns of the second are forced to +8 and -8, and `check_domain` verifies that some scaled product actually leaves the destination's range for the integer cases. A case matrix whose clamp never fires is a clamp nobody checked.
do_not_copy_when: Your scale is not a power of two. The float19 parameter field is what carries it, and reproducing that packing independently is a separate piece of work this example does not do. A passing run here says nothing about an arbitrary scale.

You are after accumulation accuracy. Every input is a small integer, so the dot product is exact before scaling -- which is the point, because it isolates the conversion. Real FP16 accumulation error is a different question.
You are relying on the offset being applied before the rounding. It is not. Two conventions exist and this one rounds first; a requantization ported from the other convention disagrees on every tie.

entries.title: Quantized L0C-to-UB transfers through a CvMutex handoff
entries.surface: Tensor.requant(scale=, offset=).subblk(0) and Tensor.relu() on an L0C accumulator stored into a UB tensor; CvMutex(id, depth=, src_end_pipe=Pipe.FIX, dst_end_pipe=Pipe.V) with lock / ready / wait / free; GetSubBlockIdx() guarding the GM publication; a kernel(mode="mix") launch
study_for: The handoff, not the arithmetic, is the subject. `CvMutex` with `src_end_pipe=Pipe.FIX` and `dst_end_pipe=Pipe.V` bridges the cube fixpipe's store into UB and the vector side's read-back, in four beats. Both vector participants run all four; only subblock 0 writes GM, guarded by `GetSubBlockIdx()`. Dropping the beats in the participant that does not publish would leave the mutex unbalanced even though its output is never used.

`.subblk(0)` is required. The sources these seven cases came from omitted the rider even though their contract described a single subblock, and every conversion here carries it. A conversion without it is not the same instruction.

Byte quantization saturates twice, in an order that matters: scale, round to nearest even, clamp to the intermediate signed 9-bit range [-256, 255], add the offset, then saturate to the destination's range. An implementation that offset before the intermediate clamp, or skipped it, disagrees on the values the planted +8 and -8 rows produce.

The scale is truncated to FixP19 before it is applied, and the reference does that truncation explicitly with a `0xFFFFE000` mask. At 0.5 and 0.25 the truncation is the identity -- `check_domain` asserts exactly that -- so it changes no value here while stating the rule that would matter for a scale where it did.

The split case keeps the full L0C pitch. `l0c[0:16, :]` and `l0c[16:32, :]` are two conversions of one 32-row accumulator into two 16-row UB tensors, through two independent mutexes, and the GM output is written in two halves. Reading the wrong 16 rows duplicates one half and loses the other, which the whole-output comparison sees twice.
do_not_copy_when: You are leaving out the subblock rider. It is required, and its absence is not a simplification.
Your scale is not exact under FixP19. Then the truncation is part of the answer and needs its own reference; nothing here establishes how an arbitrary scale rounds.

Your operands are not small integers. The domain is [-8, 8] integral values, which is what makes the products and the FP16 results exact. Non-integral operands, infinities and NaNs are outside this example.

You want the two vector participants to do different work. Here both run the mutex beats and one publishes. A genuine split of the vector work across subblocks is a different ownership arrangement, and this example's guard would be the wrong shape for it.

entries.title: The A2/A3 cube-to-vector bridge, through a two-slot GM workspace
entries.surface: GMBuff(f32, [32, 16], slots=2) as the bridge; CvMutex(0, depth=1, src_end_pipe=Pipe.FIX, dst_end_pipe=Pipe.MTE2) with lock / ready / wait / free; GetSubBlockIdx() row ownership; matmul into L0C stored to GM and read back to UB with MTE2; muls on the vector side; kernel(mode="mix") from the a2 or a3 facade
study_for: Why this kernel exists at all: A5 can move an L0C accumulator straight into UB, and A2/A3 cannot. The result therefore goes out to GM and comes back, and the extra round trip is the whole difference between the two families' cube-to-vector handoff.

`CvMutex(..., src_end_pipe=Pipe.FIX, dst_end_pipe=Pipe.MTE2)` names the two pipes at the ends of the handoff: the fixpipe writing GM, MTE2 reading it back. That is what the mutex is ordering, and the slot is returned only after *both* vector readers have finished -- not after either one.

`GetSubBlockIdx() * 16` is how each vector participant finds its own half of a 32-row product. Both halves are compared together, and `check_domain` refuses a case where either half is all zero, since a participant whose result is zeros cannot be told from one that never ran.

Three beats over two slots means the third beat reuses the first slot, so the mutex has something to hold back. `compare` reports which beat and which half disagreed, because for this kernel that localizes the fault immediately.

The operands are integers in [-4, 4] with K = 16 and the vector side multiplies by two, so every result is an exact integer well inside FP32 -- which is what makes the byte comparison legitimate, and `check_domain` says so.
do_not_copy_when: You are on A5. The direct L0C-to-UB route exists there and this GM round trip is a cost you do not need; the A5 arrangement is a separate example with its own mutex and its own pipes.
You expect the slot back after one reader. Both vector participants read every slot here, and the mutex is what enforces that.
Your operands are not exactly representable. The byte comparison rests on that; ordinary data needs a tolerance and a reference that states one.
Your geometry is not 32x16x16 over three beats. The slot size, the subblock split and the reuse pattern are all sized for it.

entries.title: Vector-cube-vector ownership, compact NZ publication and FIX destination pitch
entries.surface: kernel(mode="mix") with VcMutex over an L1 producer ring and CvMutex over each vector consumer ring, lock / ready / wait / free on both; GetSubBlockIdx() row ownership; MaskReg(dtype, MaskType.LOWHALF) strided stores; Tensor[...].nz() compact publication at an explicit row pitch; TBuff multi-slot staging; matmul into L0C and an aligned column subview of a UB allocation as a FIX destination
study_for: Addresses, not arithmetic. The narrow cases multiply the published tile by a 64x64 identity matrix, so the FP32 output *is* a readback of where every element landed. The labels are dyadic and exactly representable in both FP16 and BF16, which is what makes a byte comparison legitimate and a wrong address unmistakable rather than a small numeric difference.

`source[row, :]` loads all 128 allocated lanes and `MaskReg(dtype, LOWHALF)` limits only the store to the first 64. The other 64 source lanes are initialized to -97 on purpose: they are read every beat and must not reach the destination. Shrinking the row allocation to 64 to 'match the output' is a different program, and the guard values are how you find out.

The staging allocation is `[9, 128]` -- nine physical rows for eight live ones, room for eight NZ columns where four are published. `main.py` compares the whole allocation byte for byte as a second named output, so the padding row of each live column and all four guard columns are checked to still hold -13. The identity readback alone would accept a tile that had written over them.

`--fault` builds four deliberately broken kernels and reports which comparison catches each: `missing_mask` stores full-VL and writes -97 into the guard columns (the identity output can still agree -- only the capture catches it), `wrong_pitch` stores at pitch 8 while publication consumes pitch 9, `missing_ready` lets the cube wait with no publication token, and `compact_destination` writes a FIX result at a compacted stride. A fault that is *not* caught is reported as a defect in the checks, which is the point of having the probe inside the unit.

A FIX destination keeps its parent's physical row pitch. In `fix_pitched_columns` the parent is `[16, 256]` FP32, so rows start every 1024 bytes and the two column views at bytes 0 and 512. Both starts are 32-byte aligned and neither view is contiguous: alignment and contiguity are separate properties, and a compact alias would reduce the pitch to 512 and write the wrong rows.

The three FIX cases are a set, and reading them together is what they are for. `fix_contiguous` is the control; `fix_pitched_columns` is two views of one allocation; `fix_independent_ubs` is two allocations assembled only in GM. Every destination byte is read back after each of the two writes, so 'the first write left the right half poisoned' and 'the second write preserved the first' are both observed rather than assumed.

Three storage slots do not grant permission to overwrite a slot still in use. The mutex beats are what grant it, and both vector participants run all of them -- including, in a `single8` case, the participant whose eight rows are zeros. Dropping the beats in the participant that contributes no data leaves the ring unbalanced.

Where a `free` belongs, derived rather than placed at the end of the body. `vector_to_cube.free()` sits *after* `cube_to_vector.ready()`: the L1 tile's last reader is the matmul, and the matmul is only finished once its product has been drained into the UB slot. The FIX family says the same thing one level out -- `published.free()` then `initialized.free()`, innermost buffer first. Read each `free` off the last read of its own buffer.

`guards=` and `depth=` both appear here, and which one is right is a property of the mutex rather than a style. `roundtrip` writes `VcMutex(0, guards=left)` and `CvMutex(1, guards=middle)`, so the credit count is read out of the buffer's own type and cannot drift from it. The narrow and FIX families state `depth=` instead, because a mutex that does not hand over exactly one named buffer has no single type to read it from.
do_not_copy_when: You are reading this as an attention kernel or a performance recommendation. It is an address and ownership example; correct packing and a LOWHALF store imply nothing about speed, and no timing claim is made here.

Your labels are not exactly representable in your storage format. The byte comparison depends on that; with ordinary data you would need a tolerance, and a tolerance hides exactly the small address errors this example exists to expose.

You are treating LOWHALF as a substitute for a cast-and-store contract. A FP32-to-b16 cast can produce a sparse PART layout whose store needs downsampling; that is a different rule and nothing here establishes it.

You are declaring a compact alias for a column subview of a pitched allocation. It reduces the row pitch and writes the wrong rows. `--fault compact_destination` is that mistake, kept as a model-only mutation -- do not run any `--fault` build on hardware.

You need `fix_pitched_columns` on the pto_isa backend. Source emission refuses it at `dma.l0c_to_ub`: keeping the parent pitch makes the view declare the whole 16x256 extent while its origin is 128 elements in, so 4096 declared elements meet 3968 remaining. cce and pypto_pro both emit it -- the PyPTO adapter narrows a native Tile's valid extent rather than re-declaring storage. The case is skipped on pto_isa with the reason printed, because shrinking the declaration would defeat the subject of the case.

entries.title: A transfer's alignment tail, filled with a literal pad
entries.surface: gm_to_ub_pad(dst, src, n_burst=, burst_len_element=, src_stride_element=, dst_stride=, pad=) -- the pad keyword that finishes a burst's 32-byte alignment tail; CeilDiv / GetVecNum / GetVecIdx partitioning rows over participants
study_for: Where the pad actually lives. The backend prints `pad` into the `set_mov_pad_val` SPR before the transfer, which is where AscendC's own `DataCopyPadGm2UBImpl` puts it: mode state around the instruction, not an operand of it. Drop the keyword and the tail is not zeroed -- it keeps whatever the destination already held, which is the difference between a defined output and a plausible one.

Why the numbers are 9 and 16. Nine FP32 values are 36 bytes; the destination tile is 16 FP32, 64 bytes, two whole 32-byte blocks. The tail is the 28 bytes from 36 up to 64, and it exists because the transfer unit works in blocks while the burst length does not have to. A different dtype or a different burst moves that boundary, which is why the cases compare the whole tile rather than the copied part.

Why -1.5 and not 0. The value is 0xBFC00000, and `check_domain` refuses to run if the input carries it. That is what makes the comparison able to tell three states apart: a copied byte, a padded byte, and a byte nothing wrote -- the destination arrives NaN-poisoned, so the third one is visible too.

Only a literal pad is reachable. A run-time value raises `CceGap` at its source span: the SPR takes the value's bit pattern and the printer bitcasts it at compile time. The refusal is the API telling you where the boundary is, rather than the emitter inventing a store to get around it.
do_not_copy_when: You expect an unwritten tail to be zero. It is not, on any path here. Either you carry a pad value or you accept whatever the destination held, and the second one is only safe if you can name who wrote it last.

Your pad has to depend on the data. The instruction takes a compile-time bit pattern. A data-dependent fill is a separate vector store into the tail, with the event that orders it against the burst -- a different kernel, not a keyword change.

You are reusing the row partition without the row count. `CeilDiv(ROWS, GetVecNum())` with `ROWS = 4` divides four rows over the participants this launch has; on one participant that is all four. Copying the two lines into a kernel with a different row count, or more than one participant, changes which rows each core owns and the comparison here would not have caught it.

entries.title: A local UB ring at two, three and four slots, with both events explicit
entries.surface: DBuff / TBuff / QBuff and DEvent / TEvent / QEvent selected together by depth; event(Pipe.MTE2, Pipe.MTE3) for readiness and event(Pipe.MTE3, Pipe.MTE2, preset=True) for availability; buffer[beat] slot selection; api.unroll over a static batch expansion
study_for: Both directions are written out, and only one of them is obvious. `ready` (MTE2 to MTE3) publishes a filled slot -- the dependency everyone remembers. `available` (MTE3 to MTE2, `preset=True`) is the reverse one: it starts with one token per slot and stops the producer from refilling a slot whose consumer has not read it yet. A ring with only the first event is a ring that overwrites live data as soon as the producer gets ahead.

Depth selects a matched set. `(DBuff, TBuff, QBuff)[depth - 2]` and `(DEvent, TEvent, QEvent)[depth - 2]` are chosen together, and `buffer[beat]` picks the slot for absolute beat `beat` -- so the wraparound is the buffer's arithmetic, not the kernel's. The row count is fixed at `2 * depth + 1`, which is two full batches plus one row, so every slot is reused and the tail batch is partial.

The batch expansion is static. `for batch in api.unroll(3)` with `count = Min(depth, iterations - batch * depth)` gives three unrolled batches whose last one has a single row; the producer loop fills `count` slots before the consumer loop stores them. That producer-then-consumer shape is what makes the outstanding depth equal to the slot count rather than one.

Row `i` of the input is centred on `10 * i`, and `check_domain` refuses an input where consecutive rows are not far apart. That is a deliberate diagnostic choice: a slot reused one beat too early produces a row from the wrong batch, so the failure prints as data centred on the wrong row number instead of as a small difference nobody can localise.

`--missing-event` is the negative control and it is also the clearest statement of what the two model launchers cover. With `ready` removed, pipesim reports a real UB hazard on every case, because the consumer's read of a slot is no longer ordered after the producer's write of it. `sim` passes every case unchanged -- it interprets the kernel sequentially and models no pipes at all. A green `sim` run says nothing about synchronisation, and this is the two-line way to see that.
do_not_copy_when: You need a cross-core rendezvous. Neither event here crosses cores: both order pipes inside one vector participant. Two cores that must meet need `bar_all()` or a GM protocol, and nothing in this folder establishes one.
Your ring is in GM rather than UB. That is a different example -- `buffer_ring` covers a GM workspace ring with local autosync -- and the event pipes there are not MTE2/MTE3 in the same arrangement.

Your depth is not 2, 3 or 4. The buffer and event classes are a static, supported set; `make_ring(0)` raises rather than synthesising a ring. A deeper pipeline needs a different mechanism, not a bigger number here.

You want the events elided. `auto_sync()` would insert what it can infer, and this unit deliberately does not use it for these two dependencies: the point is the explicit form, including the reverse event that an inference pass has no way to know you wanted.

entries.title: A BF16 exponent field to an 8-bit code, and back, by hand
entries.surface: shiftls / shiftrs on a reinterpreted register; cast narrowing u16 to u8 with RegLayout.ZERO; pack(dense, sparse, HighLowPart.LOWEST) and ub_to_reg_unpack; compare + select patching one value; reg_to_ub_normal through a MaskType.LOWEST128 mask
study_for: There is no native BF16 <-> E8M0 cast here, and this is what standing in for one costs. Encoding is `shiftls 1` (the sign falls off the top), `shiftrs 8` (the exponent lands in the low byte), a u16-to-u8 narrow that leaves one code per even byte, and a `pack` that compacts them into the low half. Four instructions where a cast would be one, and each of them is visible in the output.

One decision is not arithmetic at all. Shifting a code into the BF16 exponent bits sends 255 to 0x7F80, which is +inf; the operation this sequence stands in for yields the canonical NaN 0x7FC0. So the kernel compares against 0x7F80 and selects the NaN -- a patch, written out, rather than a rounding subtlety. `check_domain` asserts the mapping on the reference so the intent cannot drift.

The physical destination is twice the logical one. `DIST_NORM_B8` writes a whole register even under a prefix mask, so the encode kernel's UB destination is 256 bytes and only its first 128 carry codes. The store's `LOWEST128` mask is what keeps the rest out of the published output, and the shape of the GM tensor is what states which half matters.

Encoding is lossy by design -- the sign and the whole mantissa go -- so the two cases are two conversions, not a round trip. The encode inputs deliberately include negatives, 1.5x powers, a subnormal and a NaN, so the fields being discarded are present rather than absent.

Both outputs are widened to INT32 for comparison: a code is an integer, a BF16 result is its stored bits. That keeps the comparison on the carriers rather than on values, which matters because two of the interesting answers -- +0 and a NaN -- do not compare usefully as numbers.
do_not_copy_when: You are reaching for a native conversion. `e8m0 <-> bf16` is in the vendor's Cast matrix and is still a gap for an upstream reason: CANN declares the vcvt for two architectures only and its builtin refuses the target feature during the op project's device build. This sequence exists because of that.

Your codes come from the legacy host MX-scale helper. Its mapping is different -- code 0 is 2^-127 and code 255 is +inf -- so the two encodings disagree at exactly the two values this unit checks most carefully.
You expect to recover a value you encoded. The exponent is all that survives. A round trip through these two kernels returns a power of two, not the input.

entries.title: A2/A3 fixpipe byte quantization and FP16 dequantization straight from L0C to GM
entries.surface: Tensor.requant(scale=, offset=) on an FP32 or INT32 L0C accumulator stored directly into a GM tensor of the destination dtype -- int8, uint8 and float16 -- with no UB staging; one kernel(mode="cube") launch per conversion on the shared A2/A3 vocabulary
study_for: The destination is GM and there is no UB anywhere. The fixpipe converts as it stores, so the conversion's rules -- rounding, the intermediate clamp, the offset, the final saturation -- all happen on the way out of L0C and cannot be inspected or repaired in between.

Byte quantization saturates twice and the order matters: scale, round to nearest even, clamp to the intermediate signed 9-bit range [-256, 255], add the offset, then saturate to the destination's own range. Adding the offset before the intermediate clamp, or skipping that clamp, gives a different answer -- at the planted boundary values, visibly so.

`qf_i8` and `qf_u8` are the *same kernel* with different destination dtypes: signedness follows the dtype. Keeping both is what turns that sentence into a check, because the unsigned path clamps to [0, 255] where the signed one clamps to [-128, 127] from the same intermediate value.

The scalar scale is truncated to the top 19 FP32 bits before it is applied, and the reference performs that truncation explicitly with a `0xFFFFE000` mask. At 0.5 and 0.25 the truncation is the identity -- `check_domain` asserts exactly that -- so it changes no value here while stating the rule that would matter for a scale where it did.

`check_domain` asserts exactly which clamps each dataset reaches, in both directions. Measured: the planted and random cases drive all three byte outputs to both ends, while the source case's products span only [-86, 82] and [-111, 94] and reach nothing but the unsigned floor. So the source case establishes the arithmetic and the rounding and nothing about the clamping -- worth knowing, because on its own it would pass every comparison while testing none of the saturation this conversion is mostly about.

Every output is compared as raw bytes, the FP16 one included: the reference builds its carriers with `struct.pack('<e', ...)` and an explicit overflow-to-infinity rule. Nothing is narrowed on the host, so a carrier is compared against a carrier and a rounding difference cannot be absorbed.
do_not_copy_when: Your operands are not integer-valued and bounded. The domain is finite FP16 integers in [-1024, 1024] and INT8 values; that is what makes the products exact and the byte comparison legitimate. Non-integral operands need their own reference for the rounding.
You are applying one saturation. There are two, in a fixed order, and a single clamp to the destination range agrees with this example only where the intermediate clamp never bites.
Your scale is not exact under the FP19 truncation. Then the truncation is part of the answer and needs its own reference; nothing here establishes how an arbitrary scale rounds.
You need the INT32-to-UINT8 path. The corrected sources have no unsigned entry for the integer accumulator, and this example does not claim one.
You are publishing through UB. This is the direct-GM path; the L0C-to-UB arrangement is a separate example with its own ownership handoff, and neither establishes the other.

entries.title: A5 fixpipe scaled casts to BF16, FP32, E4M3 and HiFloat8 straight from L0C to GM
entries.surface: Tensor.requant(scale=) on an FP32 or INT32 L0C accumulator stored directly into a GM tensor of the destination dtype -- bfloat16, float32, float8_e4m3fn and UINT8 HiFloat8 carriers under two rounding policies -- with no UB staging; one kernel(mode="cube") launch per conversion
study_for: The cube operands are FP16 and the HiFloat8 encoders consume the *FP32* L0C value after the scale. The accumulator's width is not the operands' width, and these two outputs are where that distinction is observable rather than notional.

`hif8_ta` and `hif8_hybrid` are the same value under two rounding policies, and `check_domain` refuses a case in which the two references agree everywhere -- otherwise the pair that exists to distinguish the policies would be two copies of one check.

`scaled_f32` is the control the two casts are read against: the same scaled accumulator, kept at full width. It is also the only output with a tolerance, and for a stated reason -- the host product is FP64 while the device accumulates in FP32 in its own order, so the bound covers the accumulation and not the conversion. The five carrier outputs have no tolerance at all.

The scalar scale is truncated to the top 19 FP32 bits before it is applied. 0.5 is exact under that truncation and `check_domain` asserts it, so the truncation changes no value here while the rule stays stated for a scale where it would.

`boundaries` plants products on each format's seams rather than sampling near them: the E4M3 lattice edges 448 and 464, BF16 rounding ties, powers of two down to 2**-22, and one value chosen to be the exact FP32 predecessor of 16 after the product and the scale. A generated case cannot be relied on to land on any of those.

`corrected` is the only case whose products are not exact -- Gaussian FP16 operands at the corrected helper's own M32 N64 K64 geometry. Keeping it alongside the two exact cases is what separates 'the conversion is right' from 'the conversion is right on exactly representable values'.
do_not_copy_when: Your operands are not finite and bounded by 1024 in FP16. That bound is what keeps the FP32 accumulation and the format conversions inside their stated domains, and it is checked.
Your scale is not exact under the FP19 truncation. Then the truncation is part of the answer and needs its own reference; nothing here establishes how an arbitrary scale rounds.
You expect one HiFloat8 rounding policy to stand for the other. They are separate entries because they differ, and a case where they did not differ is refused.

You want the other direct-GM modes on this device. Five more live in the `cube_quant` example at its own pin, and the L0C-to-UB arrangement is `cube_quant_ub`. Neither establishes this path, and this one establishes neither of theirs.

You are reading `scaled_f32`'s tolerance as a conversion tolerance. It covers the FP32 accumulation order against an FP64 host product; the conversions themselves are compared as carriers with no room at all.

entries.title: GM views by element stride, and an overlapping write
entries.surface: GM.view(shape, strides=, offset=) as the source and the destination of a transfer; bar_mte3() between two writes to one buffer; a rank-three view flattened row-major into a rank-two destination
study_for: What `view` counts in. `x.view([4, 32], strides=[48, 1], offset=8)` is elements throughout -- 48 is the padded row pitch, 1 the column step, 8 the starting element -- and it describes a window rather than materialising a copy.
