The same call on the destination, `o.view([4, 32], strides=[48, 1], offset=16)`, is what makes the second write land on columns 16-47 without any address arithmetic in the body.

Why the gather case declares a wider UB tile than its data. The view reads 12 elements per row, but the tile is `[4, 16]`: 16 FP32 values are 64 bytes, two whole 32-byte blocks, and the UB port steps in those blocks. Sizing the tile to the data would be the natural mistake, and the transfer that follows -- `o <<= ub[:, 0:12]` -- is where the extra columns get dropped again.

The overlap case is about order, and the barrier in it is worth being precise about. Both writes are UB-to-GM transfers, so both are tasks on the MTE3 pipe, and same-pipe order is issue order: removing `bar_mte3()` still passes pipesim, on every case. The barrier is there because the ordering matters and the source says so, not because the model needs it to -- which is exactly the kind of claim a green pipesim run cannot make for you.

How the rank-three view is checked without trusting it. `x.view([2, 2, 8], strides=[96, 16, 1])` walks two outer steps of 96 elements, two inner steps of 16, and eight contiguous elements, landing row-major in `[4, 8]`. The reference does not model a view at all: it flattens the input and takes four eight-element slices at 0, 16, 96 and 112. Two independent statements of the same 32 elements, compared byte for byte.
do_not_copy_when: You need the non-unit-stride write, not the read. Every view here is a strided *read* plus a contiguous or whole-window write. A strided destination is a different consumer and the backend refuses it at the source span rather than emitting something plausible; nothing in this folder exercises it, so a passing run says nothing about it.

You are relying on the barrier for cross-core ordering. This unit launches one vector participant (`block_dim=1`), so the only ordering it establishes is within one core's MTE3 stream. Two cores writing overlapping GM bytes need `bar_all()` or an event, and pipesim does check that -- for a kernel that actually has it.

You want to copy the UB tile shapes. They are chosen for the 32-byte block granularity of these exact widths. A different dtype or a different column count changes which tile is a whole number of blocks, and the tail you would get is not the tail these cases compare.

entries.title: The host carrier codecs, against bit references built from the formats themselves
entries.surface: ascriptor.dtypes: pack_signed_int4_to_int32 and unpack_int32_to_signed_int4, fp4_e2m1_to_fp32 / fp32_to_fp4_e2m1, fp4_e1m2_to_fp32 / fp32_to_fp4_e1m2, e8m0_to_fp32 / fp32_to_e8m0, hif8_to_fp32, fp32_to_hif8 and fp16_to_hif8 with saturate= and nan_to_zero=; one kernel(mode="vec") carrier transport
study_for: These are *host* functions, and the example says so rather than dressing them up. `ascriptor.dtypes` converts between host tensors and the packed carrier formats; the only thing running on the device is a transport that moves all 256 carriers through UB unchanged.

Every comparison is exhaustive over the one-byte code space, which at these widths is possible: 256 carriers decoded and re-encoded for each FP4 lattice, for E8M0 and for HiFloat8. An exhaustive check needs no argument about which values were chosen.
The FP4 round trip preserves both zero signs, so every physical carrier maps back to itself -- decode then encode is the identity on all 256 bytes, not on 255 of them.

The HiFloat8 encoder is checked at every interval midpoint and at both of its floating-point neighbours, across two source dtypes and all four combinations of `saturate` and `nan_to_zero`. A rounding rule that ties the wrong way changes exactly the midpoints, which is why they are where the inputs are.

reference.py imports no codec and no DSL, which `tools/api_examples.py --check` enforces. It builds each table from the format's own definition -- an exponent and fraction class enumeration for HiFloat8, literal lattices for FP4, integer shifts for int4 -- so agreement is evidence about the library rather than the library agreeing with itself.
do_not_copy_when: You are looking for device conversion instructions. These are host functions; the device casts live in their own examples, with their own rounding policies and their own layouts.
You need a NaN payload preserved. HiFloat8's NaN code decodes to a NaN whose payload is unspecified, and the comparison treats NaN as NaN for that reason.
You expect E8M0 byte 255 to be a NaN. This legacy host helper treats it as infinity, which is stated here rather than assumed.
Your HiFloat8 needs Hybrid or SSR rounding. The reference here is the away-from-zero policy only; the others are outside it.

entries.title: Independent K and V slot lifetimes across two cube products
entries.surface: DBuff and Tensor L1 allocations chosen per slot policy; DEvent and SEvent set and waited outside auto_sync() for the K load's readiness and reverse availability; CvMutex and VcMutex for the three cross-side handoffs; two matmul calls with splitk=64 and splitn=64 shortcut partitioning; a vf() FP32-to-b16 cast between them; kernel(mode="mix") at one or three mixed cores
study_for: Who reads a buffer *last* is what decides how many slots it needs. K in L1 is retired by QK's final L1-to-L0B fragment; V in L1 stays alive until the PV that runs a beat later. Same size, same writer, different lifetime -- and that is why `small_k1v2p2` gives K one slot and V two. The three small cases exist as a set: dropping either the K2 or the sequential control leaves the claim unmeasured.

The K load's readiness and reverse availability events are written out explicitly, outside `auto_sync()`. That is deliberate: with autosync covering them, removing the edge would be repaired automatically and the negative control would prove nothing. `--fault missing_k_available` removes it and the functional simulator still produces bit-exact output -- only the pipe model's WAR hazard check sees it. The probe asserts both halves, so the lesson cannot quietly decay into 'sim catches it'.

`--fault reuse_v_early` is the numeric counterpart: V drops to one slot under a lookahead policy, and the independent reference finds thousands of wrong result elements while every guard row and the final drain stay exact. That pattern -- wrong in the middle, right at the edges -- is what premature reuse looks like, as opposed to a broken product.

`--fault oversized_k2v2p2` is the capacity negative. K2/V2/P2 at N=D=256 needs 532,480 bytes through V against the A5 profile's 524,288, and it is refused while lowering with a located `addr_alloc` overflow. Capacity is checked where it is decided, not inferred from a table.

Thirty-two output rows, of which sixteen are results and sixteen are guards with a distinct label each. Both vector participants write eight result rows; `bf16_idle` runs three cores for one item so two of them execute no beats at all. Comparing results and guards together is what turns a lost store or a stale slot into a failure instead of a plausible number.

The reference is a dense FP64 product that rounds the first result to b16 explicitly, exactly where the kernel's vector cast does. It imports no DSL, lowering or packing helper -- so agreement is evidence about the device, and the b16 rounding step is stated rather than inherited.
do_not_copy_when: You are reading this as attention. There is no softmax, no scale, no causal mask and no accumulation between beats; it is the storage skeleton such a kernel would sit on, and nothing here is a performance claim or a recommended slot count for one.

Your K and V share an allocation. A sibling contract may permit numerically equal K and V in one buffer, which adds PV to that buffer's reader set and changes every lifetime here. This example asserts the opposite premise -- separate storage and different values -- and its slot counts follow from it.
You are relying on autosync for a cross-beat reuse edge. It would hide exactly the mistake this example is built to expose; the events are explicit here for that reason.

Your geometry is not one of the six. Width is 64 or 256, M is 16, five beats. The shortcut partitioning is sized so each largest B fragment is 32,768 bytes and fits one of the two 32-KiB L0 slots; a different width has to redo that arithmetic.

You need the timing story. Model cycles measure no device latency, and the historical acquisitions that once accompanied this example showed no stable ranking between the policies -- fewer slots was slower at one geometry and faster at another. Slot reduction is a capacity argument here, not a speed one.

entries.title: Typed indexed gathers and scatters, and byte-offset block gathers
entries.surface: ub_to_reg_gather and ub_to_reg_gatherb with a UINT16/UINT32/UINT64 index register loaded by ub_to_reg_normal; reg_to_ub_scatter with unique destinations and an explicit STORE-to-STORE barrier; reinterpret() to read a signed index row as unsigned; fourteen kernel(mode="vec") entries over element widths 1/2/4/8
study_for: The index register's element width and the data's element width are separate choices, and the fourteen entries are the cross product worth knowing: 16-bit data with UINT16 indices, 32-bit with UINT32, and 64-bit data reachable through *either* a UINT32 or a UINT64 index register. Picking the index width from the data width is the mistake the `gather_b64_u32` / `gather_b64_u64` pair exists to prevent.

A byte gather zero-extends. An INT8 source byte arrives in an INT16 destination with a zero high byte, and the signed and unsigned byte cases sit side by side precisely so a sign extension is visible as a wrong answer in one of them. `check_domain` asserts every extension byte of the reference is zero, so the property is stated and not just implied by agreement.

A byte scatter consumes source byte `2 * k` for index lane k, because the index lanes are 16-bit. The even source bytes are the payload; a dense byte read is a different program with the same shape. The kernel zeroes the whole destination first and keeps the explicit STORE-to-STORE barriers around the scatter.

GatherB indices are byte offsets, not element counts -- eight aligned 32-byte blocks out of a 512-byte source, each named by its byte address. `check_domain` requires them aligned and fully inside the source, so an index expressed in elements fails the check rather than reading a shifted block.

Only the defined index lanes are consumed: thirty-two for 64-bit data behind a UINT32 register, eight for GatherB. `unused_index_zero` and `unused_index_high` share a seed and differ only in what the undefined lanes hold -- 0 against 2147483647 -- and main.py compares the two runs' outputs to each other. Neither case alone can make that statement, which is why running them together is part of the example rather than an accident of the matrix.

Every result is compared as its 256 raw payload bytes, and the reference is Python byte-list addressing. No cast, codec or library helper stands between either side and the bytes, so a signed carrier, a set high bit and a float bit pattern all survive the comparison intact -- including the extension zeros and the untouched scatter holes.
do_not_copy_when: Your scatter has duplicate destinations. They are unique here on purpose: the order in which two writers reach one destination is not declared, so nothing in this example establishes what that produces. Repeated *gather* indices are fine and `repeated_gather` exercises them.
Your active indices can leave the declared source or destination. Only the defined lanes are range-checked, and an out-of-range active index is rejected rather than clamped.
You want 64-bit block movement. The corrected GatherB bodies here are b8/b16/b32 only; the 64-bit block width lives in its own example and is not reachable from these entries.
You are generalizing to a masked scatter. This byte scatter is unmasked. A partial predicate over the same instruction is a separate study with its own evidence, and nothing here covers it.

Your row is not one complete typed row. Each movement declares its exact source, index and destination row, and one vector participant. A partial row or a second participant would need its own ownership statement.

entries.title: Whole-row gather addressed by a value in memory
entries.surface: Var.GetValueFrom on a UB cell used as a GM row subscript; two tables gathered at their own row widths; a runtime live count driving both a guarded write and a clamped one
study_for: An index is a value until it is in a cell. The whole index table crosses once (`slots <<= index`) and each slot is then read with `GetValueFrom` from UB, because a per-slot GM scalar read would be one MTE2 round trip per row. The view handed to `GetValueFrom` has to be narrowed to the single element -- it takes the first element of whatever view it is given, so a wider one reads `slots[0, 0]` every trip and produces no diagnostic at all.

Each table is gathered at its own row width, and the two ways of getting that wrong are not equally visible. `DK` is 64 and `DV` is 48, so no single width addresses both. Because the two tables are declared separately here, a `DK`-wide read of `v_table` is rejected outright -- `slice [0:64) outside extent 48`. The layout `Dv < Dk` usually comes from is a `DV` prefix of a `DK`-wide row, and there the same mistake is accepted silently and returns the next field's columns. The sidecar check in the pytest tree records both diagnostics.

The gather is unconditional, so padding is dereferenced too. Every one of the sixteen slots is copied, which means a padding index must be a legal row of its table: what makes a slot padding is that nothing downstream reads its result, not that the copy was skipped. Three cases fill the padding differently -- row zero, the far row 127, a repeat of a live row -- and `k_rows` / `v_rows` record where each landed.

Why the clamp is in here on purpose. The destination has `live` real rows while the loop runs the padded slot count, so slots at and past `live` have nowhere to be written. `guarded` uses the runtime comparison `if s < live:`. `clamped` writes `min(s, live - 1)`, which is the reflex an out-of-range write invites: the address stays inside the tensor and every padding slot lands on the last real row, so that row ends up holding the last padding slot's data. The reference computes the same corruption, so the example proves the trap instead of asserting it.

Two choices that make a failure readable rather than just red. Column zero of each table holds the row's own number, so a wrong index prints as a wrong row label; and all four destinations arrive filled with 1024.0, outside both tables' value range, so a row nothing wrote is distinguishable from a row written wrongly. `live` is a runtime input, not a constant, because in a real kernel the tail's row count comes from metadata and the guard has to be a runtime comparison.
do_not_copy_when: You are looking for an attention operator. This is the addressing step of one, and nothing else: no score, no mask, no softmax, no reduction. Taking it as a template for the rest of that kernel is the mistake it is most likely to invite.

Your rows are a prefix of a wider record. Then the separate-table protection this unit relies on is gone: a too-wide read of a `DV` prefix inside a `DK`-wide row is accepted and silently returns the neighbouring field. The check has to move to the host or to the layout in that case; a passing run here does not transfer.
You were going to clamp the destination row. That is the defect this unit reproduces and predicts. Guard the write, or partition the slots so the tail has somewhere to go.

You need what a sparse-attention kernel needs around this. Not covered here, and not implied by it: a bottom-right causal geometry whose fully masked rows must emit zeros without producing NaN, grouped query attention sharing one gather across the queries of a `(b, n2)` pair, column blocking of the `PV` product when `Dv < Dk`, and any of those combined with an online softmax.

entries.title: A ReLU at the fixpipe feeding an L0C accumulator back into L1
entries.surface: Tensor.relu() on an L0C accumulator stored directly into an FP16 L1 tile; SEvent(Pipe.FIX, Pipe.MTE1) set and waited explicitly inside auto_sync(); two matmul calls in one kernel(mode="cube") launch, the second consuming the first's result
study_for: The feedback path is the subject: an FP32 L0C accumulator becomes an FP16 L1 tile through `l0c_mid.relu()` and is consumed by the next `matmul` in the same launch, without passing through UB or GM. The conversion, the clamp and the store are one fixpipe operation.

`SEvent(Pipe.FIX, Pipe.MTE1)` is set and waited by hand even though the body runs inside `auto_sync()`. Those are the two pipes actually involved -- the fixpipe writes the L1 tile and MTE1 reads it back for the second product -- and naming them is what orders the two.

One cell of the output is the ReLU witness, and it was planted. `x[0]` is all ones and `y[1]` all minus ones, so the intermediate at (0, 1) is -32 before the clamp; `z[0]` is zero except `z[0, 1] = 1`, which reads that single cell into `output[0, 0]`. A kernel that dropped the clamp prints -32 there instead of 0, and `compare` prints that cell on every run. Without the planted rows a random signed input might clamp nothing at all.

The bitwise comparison is earned rather than assumed. Operands are integers in [-3, 3], so the first product is at most 288 in magnitude -- exactly representable in FP16 -- and the second product is exact in FP32. `check_domain` asserts the domain that makes each of those true, so widening the operands fails the assertion instead of silently making the comparison wrong.

The reference computes both products in integer arithmetic and clamps with `clamp_min(0)`. It calls no fixpipe helper, no conversion helper and nothing from the kernel, so agreement is evidence about the device rather than about the library agreeing with itself.
do_not_copy_when: Your intermediate can exceed the FP16 exact-integer range. The whole comparison rests on the feedback boundary being exact for this domain; past 2048 it is not, and you need a tolerance and a different reference.
Your operands are not integral. Nothing here establishes how arbitrary FP16 values round at the fixpipe conversion, and no exceptional value -- infinity, NaN, subnormal -- appears in this domain.
You are relying on auto_sync() alone to order a fixpipe write against an MTE1 read. This kernel names the event explicitly; treat that as part of the pattern, not as decoration.
Your tiles are not complete. M=N=P=16 and K=32 are fixed here, and no tail, padding or multi-core split is exercised -- a second core would need its own ownership statement.

entries.title: Ragged GMList members concatenated on the device
entries.surface: GMList[f32, ("?", 64)] as an input argument; `for t in xs:` iterating members on the device with `t.shape[0]` as each member's own extent; a dynamic GM[f32, ("N", 64)] destination with N as a runtime scalar
study_for: What the list descriptor buys. `xs` is one kernel argument standing for three separately allocated members with different row counts. The device loop `for t in xs:` reads the descriptor, and `t.shape[0]` is that member's extent -- so no host code unrolls the members into separate arguments and nothing is padded to a common shape. The two cases use different extents with the identical kernel source, which is what shows the extents are data rather than constants.

Where the concatenation actually happens. Each member's rows are moved through one 8x64 UB tile, and the destination cursor `row` is declared before the member loop and advances inside it. That single cursor crossing member boundaries is the whole difference between a concatenation and three copies that each start at row zero -- and the `ragged` case, whose members are 16, 32 and 8 rows, is the one where getting it wrong misplaces two of the three.

The destination's shape is symbolic and its extent is an argument. `GM[f32, ("N", 64)]` is declared with a name, and `N` arrives as an `i32` scalar in the same call. The host passes the summed row count, so the kernel needs no compile-time knowledge of how the members divide up.

Why the comparison is bitwise against `torch.cat`. Nothing here computes: every output byte is an input byte that moved. A tolerance would only be able to hide the two failures this unit can actually have -- a burst that never landed, or one that landed in the wrong row.
do_not_copy_when: Your member extents are not multiples of the staging tile. The loop steps `range(0, rows, 8)` with an 8-row tile and there is no tail path here at all; `check_domain` refuses such an input rather than letting a partial burst read as a pass. A ragged tail needs its own transfer with its own length.

Your members are views rather than allocations. `t[r:r+8, :]` is a contiguous burst because each member is contiguous. A member that is a slice of something wider makes that same expression a strided transfer, which is a different instruction with a different cost.

You want more than one participant writing. This launch is `block_dim=1` and one vector participant owns every row of the destination. Dividing the members across cores means deciding which core owns which output rows, and nothing in this folder establishes that.

entries.title: One tall input split into ragged GMList members
entries.surface: GMList[f32, ("?", 64)] as the destination argument, with three separately allocated members; `for t in ys:` writing each member at its own extent; a dynamic GM[f32, ("N", 64)] source with N as a runtime scalar
study_for: A `GMList` works as a destination, and the members stay distinct. The caller allocates three tensors of different heights and hands them in as one argument; the kernel returns `ys`, and the runtime gives each member back in the caller's own shape. All three are compared here -- a split whose last member was folded into the previous one would pass a check that only looked at the concatenation.

The source cursor is what makes it a split. `row` is declared before the member loop and advances inside it, so member 1 starts where member 0 stopped. Reset it per member and every member receives the input's first rows instead, which the `ragged` case -- 16, 32 and 8 out of 56 -- makes visible in two of the three members at once.

This is `list_concat` read backwards, and the pair is worth reading together: the same 8x64 staging tile, the same `for t in ...` device iteration, the same symbolic `N`. What changes is which side of the transfer the list is on, and therefore who allocates the members.

The comparison is bitwise against host slicing, and every member is NaN-poisoned before the launch. That combination is what separates the three things that can go wrong: a member nothing wrote (still NaN), a member written from the wrong offset (wrong bytes), and a member written twice (the earlier content gone).
do_not_copy_when: Your member extents are not multiples of the staging tile. The loop steps `range(0, rows, 8)` and there is no tail path; `check_domain` refuses such an input rather than letting a partial burst read as a pass.

The extents do not sum to the input's height. Nothing in the kernel checks that, and the consequence is silent: rows past the last member's end are simply never read, and the comparison here would not notice because it only looks at the members. The host owns that invariant.

You want the members to overlap, or to be slices of one allocation. Then they are not separate members and the descriptor is the wrong tool -- views of one tensor with explicit offsets say what you mean, and the ordering between writes becomes your problem rather than the list's.

entries.title: Cube products over E5M2, HiFloat8 and scale-paired MXFP4 carriers
entries.surface: matmul over float8_e5m2 operands with shortcut partitioning; HiFloat8 carriers consumed as cube operands in all four transpose pairings, each with no split, splitn=32 and splitk=32, twelve destinations from one kernel(mode="cube") launch; FP4 E2M1 against FP4 E1M2 with row-major packed E8M0 scale codes, one scale per 32 logical K values
study_for: Thirteen HiFloat8 outputs, one reference. `hif_at` and `hif_bt` are the transposes of the very operands the untransposed entries take, so all four transpose pairings and all three split policies are computing the same product by different routes. main.py also compares the thirteen to each other and prints the spread, which no comparison against the reference can produce. They are not bitwise identical and the example does not pretend they are: the spread is exactly 0 for the two encoded cases and 1.28e+02 for `finite_carriers`, whose magnitudes reach 1e9 and where splitk accumulates in a different order. The spread is checked against the same element bound, which in that case is 2.9e+06 -- so read it as a reported number, not as a tight check.

MXFP4 pairs *different* FP4 lattices on purpose: E2M1 for A and E1M2 for B. The scale is a packed E8M0 code per 32 logical K values, and `identity_scales` sets every code to 127, whose factor is exactly 1. That case is the control -- with scaling switched off, a disagreement is in the FP4 product rather than the scales -- and `check_domain` verifies the reference really is the plain decoded product there, and that a scaled case has at least two different codes.

The references decode each format from its own bit fields and multiply in FP64: a HiFloat8 code table, an E5M2 field decomposition, and literal FP4 lattices. No execution codec, kernel helper or library cast participates, which is what makes the products evidence about the cube.

`finite_carriers` builds operands from each format's code table directly rather than by encoding values, including sign variations. An encoder reaches only the codes it happens to produce; a carrier-level case reaches the ones it does not.

The bounds are per output, and none of them is tight. Measured on the functional simulator, every allclose margin prints as 0.000x and the worst relative L2 over all three cases is 3.6e-08 against the 2e-03 allowed -- four orders of magnitude of slack, even for E5M2 whose element bound is twenty-five times the others'. So the tolerances are inherited from the sources rather than measured constraints, and what actually fails here is a wrong address or a dropped operand: wrong by orders of magnitude, not by a fraction. `compare` prints both numbers on every run so that stays visible.
Every destination starts at -777 and is seeded in, and `check_domain` refuses a reference that contains that value -- so an element the cube never wrote cannot be mistaken for a product.
do_not_copy_when: Your operands are not finite in their format. The numerical domains here exclude the HiFloat8 and E5M2 non-finite codes, and that exclusion is checked: the unchecked random-byte generator this example grew out of produced hundreds of NaN and infinite products, which is why the domain is stated rather than assumed.

You need more than one MX scale block per operand. Exactly one 32-byte block per operand is exercised, selecting one scale for each 32 logical K values; a multi-block arrangement is a different addressing question.

You are assuming the transposed operand is a different logical input. It is not, here -- that is the premise. If your transposed operand holds different values, none of the thirteen-way agreement applies.

You are carrying E5M2's bound over to another format. It is loose because that entry's reviewed tolerance was loose; the HiFloat8 and MXFP4 outputs are held twenty-five times tighter, and a single shared bound would be wrong for one of them.
You want a performance statement. Split policies appear here to show they agree numerically, not to rank them; nothing here measures the cube.

entries.title: Predicate logic under an execution mask, and the counter it draws down
entries.surface: update_mask(gate, remaining) with a u32 Var counter; MaskReg(dtype, init_mode=MaskType.ALL / NONE / LOWEST32); compare(pred, reg, value, CompareMode.GT, gate); select and MaskReg.select; mask_not / mask_and / mask_or / mask_xor / mask_mov / mask_sel; mask_pack / mask_unpack; mask_interleave / mask_deinterleave
study_for: `update_mask` consumes its counter, and the last row is how you can see it. `remaining` is a `u32` Var initialised to the case's count; after `update_mask(gate, remaining)` the gate covers `min(count, 64)` lanes and the counter holds `max(count - 64, 0)`. The kernel fills a register from `remaining` and publishes it, so the mutation is observed rather than inferred from the mask bits -- which is the only way to tell a counter that was drawn down from one that was read.

At b32, a masked predicate operation clears its inactive lanes. Every destination mask in the body is initialised differently on purpose -- `MaskType.ALL` for the not/and/xor results, `NONE` for or/mov/sel -- and the reference computes `gate & ...` for all of them. Twelve rows agreeing with that is the statement: the initialisation does not survive, so no row of this output depends on it. The `prefix_0` case is where it would show if it did, because there the gate is empty and the initial value is all there would be.

The gate is an execution mask; `pred` and `short` are selector masks. `compare(pred, a, 0, GT, gate)` uses the gate to decide which lanes the compare runs on; `pred.select(one, zero)` and `select(value, a, b, gate)` use a mask to choose between two operands. The two roles are spelled similarly and mean different things, which is why both appear in row 0 and row 1.

`mask_pack` then `mask_unpack` is a lossless round trip that does not look like one. A b32 lane observes physical bit 4*i; packing moves it to 2*i, so the packed result seen at b32 is `pred[::2]` with its upper half zero -- half the predicate appears to be gone. Unpacking restores bit 4*i and the original predicate comes back whole, because the bits that b32 could not see were still there. Rows 8 and 9 are that pair, and reading row 8 alone is how you would conclude, wrongly, that pack discards.

Five prefix counts: 0, 3, 63, 64, 70. 63 is the one that catches a count rounded up to the register width; 64 is the boundary where the counter reaches exactly zero; 70 is the only case where anything is left in it.
do_not_copy_when: You expect `update_mask` to leave its counter alone. It does not, and a loop that re-reads the same Var expecting the original count will build the same mask forever.
You are relying on a mask destination's initial value. At b32 it is cleared where the gate is inactive. If you need lanes preserved, that is a different operation and this unit does not contain one.
You read row 8 as evidence that packing loses bits. It does not; row 9 recovers everything. The b32 view is what is lossy, not the pack.

Your predicate is not b32. The lane-to-physical-bit relationship -- and therefore what pack, unpack, interleave and deinterleave do to the lanes you can see -- depends on the element width. Every row here is an INT32 register.

entries.title: Mask state read across a @vf boundary, and exclusive prefix counts
entries.surface: set_mask_by_count(n) / set_mask(0, pattern) / reset_mask() at kernel scope with move_mask_spr(mask) reading them inside a @vf; unsqueeze(reg, mask) replacing a register with the exclusive prefix count of a predicate
study_for: Mask state crosses the vector-function boundary, and that is the whole point of the `spr` mode. `set_mask_by_count` and `set_mask` are called at kernel scope; `move_mask_spr` reads the result inside the `@vf`. Each observation is rendered as 7-or-0 per lane and published before the next mask is installed, so three rows read in sequence say what the state was at three moments -- the third one, with nothing set, is the check that `reset_mask` put the full mask back.

Two SPR spellings that are not interchangeable. A count sets a prefix; a pattern sets arbitrary bits. `spr_20` pairs count 20 with pattern 0xF0F -- four set, four clear, four set -- which no count can produce, and that is what makes the pair of rows a comparison rather than a repetition. `spr_1`'s pattern has only bit 0 and bit 63, so a read that lost or sign-extended the high half of the 64-bit word fails at one lane on each end.

`unsqueeze` is an exclusive prefix count, and neither of the two things its name suggests. It replaces the register's contents with the number of earlier active lanes -- not including the lane itself -- so it is not a host reshape and not a decompaction of data values. `prefix_last`, where only lane 63 is active and every lane including that one answers zero, is the case that pins the word 'exclusive' down.

Both prefix rows run the same predicate over different old register contents (the second row's data is offset by 234567). They must agree. That is how the unit states that the old value is ignored, instead of trusting that it is -- and it costs one extra row.

Three of the ten cases have all-zero expected output (`spr_0`'s first two rows, `prefix_empty`, `prefix_last`), so a zero-filled destination would let a missing publication pass. The destination arrives at -777 for exactly that reason, and the sidecar controls in the pytest tree use perturbation and an inclusive-prefix comparison for those cases rather than a zero replacement that proves nothing there.
do_not_copy_when: You wanted an inclusive prefix. This is exclusive: lane `i` answers how many lanes before `i` were active. Adding the lane's own predicate back is your arithmetic, not the instruction's.
You expect `unsqueeze` to move data. It does not touch the values -- it overwrites the register with counts. A decompaction of the data itself is a gather or a scatter, not this.

You are setting a temporary mask and not resetting it. `spr_64` is the case where forgetting would still pass, because there the temporary mask and the full mask are the same. Every other case would catch it, and so would whatever ran after your kernel.

entries.title: ND DMA: two paddings, a three-loop selection and a transpose
entries.surface: gm_to_ub_nd_dma(dst, src, loop_src_strides, loop_dst_strides, loop_sizes, loop_left_pad=, loop_right_pad=, config_left_pad=, config_right_pad=, constant_value=, nearest_value_mode=, fence=) and the gm_to_ub_nd_dma_transpose shorthand
study_for: Loop 0 is the innermost one, and every stride counts elements. The three lists are source strides, destination strides and iteration counts, in that loop order, which is why the row-selection transfer reads `[1, 2*COLS, 8*COLS]`, `[1, 32, 128]`, `[32, 4, 2]` -- 32 contiguous columns, then four rows two apart, then two blocks eight rows apart, giving rows 0, 2, ... 14 of `x[:, :32]`. Reading those three lists outside-in is the mistake that produces a plausible transfer of the wrong elements.

Two spellings of the same padding, and what picks between them. `loop_left_pad=[3, 2]` pads per loop -- three on the inner, two on the outer -- while `config_left_pad=8` is the default every loop takes when no per-loop list is given; the printer emits them into the same `NdLoops` field. The BF16 transfer uses the config form because all its loops want the same eight elements a side.

What the padded positions are filled with. `constant_value=-1.5` writes a literal, and `nearest_value_mode=True` repeats the nearest real element of that loop instead -- edge replication, which the reference states independently as `F.pad(..., mode='replicate')`. The two cases pad the same window both ways in one launch, so the difference between them is visible side by side rather than across runs.

`fence` decides what closes the transfer. The default `all` ends it with `pipe_barrier(PIPE_ALL)`; the BF16 transfer passes `fence='mte2'` instead, which scopes the wait to the transfer pipe. It is the one attribute here that changes the synchronisation rather than the data, so a copy of this line into a kernel whose next reader is not on MTE2 is a copy of the wrong thing.

The transpose is sugar, not a separate path. `gm_to_ub_nd_dma_transpose(ub_t, x[0:16, 0:32])` builds the same ND loops with the rows walking innermost; the reference is `x[:16, :32].T.contiguous()`. Comparing the whole 32x16 destination is what makes that a statement about every element rather than about the shape.
do_not_copy_when: Your destination tile is not the one these transfers were sized for. Each UB tensor here is declared at the exact padded destination shape, and the pads are counted in elements of that shape. A different width changes where the border lands and the numbers in the three lists stop describing it.

You want the BF16 path's rounding checked. Nothing here rounds: the transfer copies BF16 bytes and pads them with a value that is exact in BF16. The reference widens to FP32 only so `F.pad` can take the value, then narrows back -- a passing run says the transfer preserved bytes, not that any conversion is right.
You are after cross-core ordering. One vector participant owns every write here, so `fence` is about pipes inside a core and nothing in this folder exercises two cores touching the same destination.

entries.title: Physical cast layouts: UINT2, FP4, dual FP8 and HiFloat8 both directions
entries.surface: Ten kernel(mode="vec") cast entries: BF16 to packed UINT2 carriers and back with an explicit padding row, BF16 to FP4 E1M2 nibble pairs, one source row cast to float8_e5m2 and float8_e4m3fn in a single launch, and HiFloat8 carriers decoded to FP32/FP16 and encoded from them under two rounding policies
study_for: Every reference is built from the format's bit layout -- a code table, shifts and masks -- and calls no library codec. That is what makes agreement evidence about the cast instruction instead of a comparison of the library with itself, and it is why the boundary cases can be trusted.

Four cases are exhaustive rather than sampled: `fp4_all_finite_bf16` enumerates all 65024 finite BF16 words, and the two `*_all_bits` cases enumerate all 65536 half-precision words. At these widths the whole input space fits in a run, so a rounding boundary cannot be missed by construction -- and a sampled case would never establish the same thing.

The two HiFloat8 rounding policies, `ta` and `hybrid`, appear as separate entries over the same source words. Their pair is the subject: the codes agree everywhere except where the policies differ, so running one alone tells you nothing about which one you have.

`uint2_unpack` takes its padding as an explicit argument, and three cases hand it 0, 0xA5 and random bytes. 0xA5 is chosen because all four of its 2-bit fields are non-zero, so padding that leaked into a result is unmistakable. main.py compares the three runs' outputs to each other -- no single case can state that the padding does not matter.

`fp8_dual` writes E5M2 and E4M3 from one launch, so both lattices see exactly the same source values. `fp8_boundaries` gives it every representable value of both lattices, every midpoint, the neighbour on each side of each, and the infinities and NaN -- which is where a tie that rounds the wrong way, or a saturation where an overflow belongs, becomes visible.

The comparison is byte equality with exactly one exemption: two NaNs agree whatever their payloads hold, because the payload of a NaN result is not specified by these formats. Nothing else is loosened -- and since HiFloat8 has a single zero code, the sign of zero never arises here, while anywhere else a flipped zero sign would be a different byte and a failure.
do_not_copy_when: You are treating a NaN payload as defined. It is not, which is the one place this example's comparison is not a byte comparison. If your kernel depends on a particular NaN payload, that dependency is outside anything established here.
Your UINT2 input is not exactly 0, 1, 2 or 3 in BF16. The packing entry accepts only those; what it does with a non-integral or out-of-range value is not covered.
Your FP4 input is not finite. The preserved domain is finite BF16, and infinities and NaNs through the FP4 packing are not part of this example.

You are assuming a padding row cannot affect an unpacked result. This example checks that it does not, across three different padding rows -- checking is the point, and a single padding value would not have made the statement.

You expect one rounding policy to stand for the other. `ta` and `hybrid` are separate entries because they differ; picking one and assuming the other matches is the mistake the pair exists to prevent.

entries.title: One radix_topk call, and the two different checks its two outputs need
entries.surface: radix_topk(values_ub, indices_ub, src_ub, count, k) over a complete [1, 4096] UB source into [1, 512] value and index tiles, with count and k as i32 kernel arguments; one kernel(mode="vec") launch
study_for: The two outputs need two different kinds of check, and that is the lesson. The k largest values are a well-defined multiset, so they have a reference and are compared after sorting -- the order the device returns them in is not part of the contract. The indices have no reference at all, because which index wins a tie is unspecified, so they are checked by their properties: in range, distinct, and each naming the lane whose bits were returned beside it.

The index check compares bits, not numbers. A value that merely equals its source numerically is not necessarily from that lane -- with ties, several lanes hold equal values -- and comparing the bit patterns is what ties a returned value to the index that claims it.

`ties` is the case that makes the distinction real. With values drawn from a pool of seven, many lanes are equal and several compete for the same rank; a comparison against a fixed index table would fail there for a correct implementation.

The source tile is always 4096 lanes with `count` live and the rest at -infinity. The padding is part of the calling convention, and `check_domain` asserts it is there -- an implementation that selected from a padded lane would be returning -infinity, which the multiset comparison catches.
The boundaries are the cases: k = 1 is the smallest selection, k = count selects everything live, and the full geometry has 4096 live lanes and 512 slots with no padding at all.
do_not_copy_when: You need a defined order, or a defined index at a tie. Neither is specified. If your caller depends on one, sort afterwards -- and be aware that the tie-breaking index is still not yours to assume.
Your source is not padded past the count. The -infinity padding is what keeps unselected lanes out of the result; leaving whatever was there before is a different program.
Your k exceeds 512 or your count exceeds 4096. Those are the tile sizes, and the parameters are checked against them before anything runs.

entries.title: Two-register groups: integer, reduction, cast, memory and complex
entries.surface: Reg(dtype, reg_num=2) and MaskReg(dtype, reg_num=2); MaskReg.update(count) tails; vand / vmod / muldstadd / shiftrs; Reg.arange; interleave / deinterleave and mask_interleave; ub_to_reg_gather / reg_to_ub_scatter; cast with CastConfig(round_mode=RoundMode.TRUNC); complex32 and complex64 registers
study_for: A group is one logical register over two physical ones, and the masks cross that seam on purpose. `reg_num=2` gives 512 bytes; the int64 tails are 47 lanes and the complex32 one is 95, so each crosses the single-register boundary (32 and 64 respectively). An implementation that applied a mask only to the first physical register passes a 32-lane test and fails every case here.

The memory variant puts two different mask semantics side by side. A masked gather clears the lanes it did not fill; a masked scatter leaves untouched destination lanes exactly as they were, which is why the kernel calls `d.fill(0)` and publishes that zero before scattering into it. Reading those three rows together is the cheapest way to learn which of the two you are dealing with.

`deinterleave(d, e, d, e)` aliases its outputs onto its inputs, and both original halves still have to be read before either is written. The row pair before it holds the interleaved values, so the recovery is checked against the original inputs rather than against a claim that the operation is reversible.

The integer ramps are based at +/-18014398509481991, past 2^54. That is a statement about the reference as much as about the kernel: a reference that computed the ramp in float64 would round the low bits away and then agree with an implementation that had also lost them. The reference builds the ramp from Python integers.

Everything is compared as `uint8` carriers. The destinations include `complex32`, `complex64` and `uint64`; concatenating their bytes is what lets one comparison cover both components of every complex lane, the low bits of every wide integer, and each lane a mask left inactive -- with a poison of 97 in every destination, so an unwritten byte is distinguishable from a deliberately cleared one.
do_not_copy_when: You are counting on a masked scatter to zero what it skipped. It does not. The destination is yours to initialise, and this unit only gets a defined answer because it does.

You are treating the non-leading reduction lanes as a device guarantee. Rows 0 to 2 of the reduce variant hold their result in lane 0 and zero elsewhere in the model; a model check does not by itself establish that on silicon.

You need the complex variants on a backend other than CCE. Their kernels say so: hardware backend support is CCE only. The PTO complex-type refusal and the PyPTO grouped-register refusal are located by the backend tests, not here, and a green run of this unit says nothing about either.

You want a single-register example. Every register here is a group, and several of the assertions exist only because it is. For the single-register behaviour of the same operations, the mask extents and boundaries would all be different numbers.

entries.title: Natural, base-two and base-ten logarithms of one register
entries.surface: Reg.ln() / Reg.log2() / Reg.log10() inside a @vf body; one Reg re-loaded per row from a UB tensor at element offsets
study_for: One primitive, three bases, and that is where the tolerance comes from. The backend has a logarithm instruction; `log2` and `log10` may be composed from `ln` and an FP32 scale multiplication. So the outputs are not bit-equal to Torch's own three functions, and saying so with a budget is more honest than either a bitwise comparison that would fail for the wrong reason or a loose one that would hide a wrong scale.

Two bounds, because one is not enough. `allclose` catches a single bad lane; a relative L2 residual over the whole output catches a uniform bias that stays inside every element's own allowance. A wrong base constant is exactly that second failure -- every lane off by the same factor -- and it would pass the element bound at these magnitudes.

The first eight lanes are chosen, not random: 1, 2, 4, 10, 100, 0.5, 0.1, 1024. At 1 all three bases answer zero; at the powers of two and ten `log2` and `log10` answer integers. A wrong scale therefore prints as a clean factor at a known lane instead of as noise spread over a thousand of them.

The domain is refused rather than defined. Zero, negatives and non-finite inputs raise in `check_domain`; nothing here claims what the primitive does with them. That is a smaller promise than it looks -- and the right size of promise for a unit whose whole subject is the finite positive case.
do_not_copy_when: Your input can be zero, negative or non-finite. This unit says nothing about those, on purpose. A kernel that must handle them needs its own decision -- a clamp, a mask, a sentinel -- and its own reference for it.

You need log2 to be exact at powers of two. It is not guaranteed to be here, because the base may be reached by scaling `ln`. If exactness at those points matters, an exponent-extraction path is a different kernel.

You are reading the row loop as a single wide operation. Each row is one register load, three logarithms and three stores; the `@vf` body walks sixteen rows at element offsets. The cost model and the register pressure are per row, not per output.

entries.title: Whole-register sum, max and min at three widths
entries.surface: cadd / cmax / cmin over a whole Reg; Reg(DT.float), Reg(DT.int), Reg(DT.int64); register stores addressed by element offset (out[0], out[cols], out[2*cols]) inside a @vf body
study_for: A whole-register reduction answers in lane 0. All nine results here are written a full register apart by element offset, so `out[0]`, `out[cols]` and `out[2 * cols]` are three rows of the destination -- the addressing is in elements of the register, not in rows of the tensor, and that is the part worth copying carefully.

The lanes that are not lane 0 are compared, not ignored. `upper` is every column but the first of the float destination, 189 lanes the model leaves zero, and the destination arrives NaN-poisoned so a lane nothing wrote is distinguishable from a lane written with zero. That distinction is the whole reason the poison is not zero.

The INT64 input carries -2^62 and 2^62 + 12345 deliberately. Both differ from the surrounding +/-2^40 values only in their upper word, so `cmax` and `cmin` at 64 bits cannot come out right by comparing low halves. Without those two plants, an implementation that reduced 32-bit halves would pass.

Only one output has a tolerance, and the reason is narrow. `sum` is an FP32 reduction, so its value depends on the order the lanes were added in; the bounds are Torch's own isclose defaults. Everything else -- both extrema, both integer widths, every zero lane -- is a byte comparison, which keeps the tolerance surface as small as the arithmetic actually requires.
do_not_copy_when: You are treating the zero lanes as a hardware guarantee. They are what the current local model produces. A model result does not by itself establish the device's defined-lane behaviour, and this unit has no card evidence for it -- run it with `--launcher aclnn` on a machine with one if you need that answer.

Your integer values can overflow the reduction width. `check_domain` refuses an input whose integer sum leaves the type, because the reference and the device would then be comparing two different defined behaviours rather than agreeing or disagreeing.

You need a deterministic float sum. It is not one, which is exactly why `sum` carries the only tolerance here. A reduction whose order you must control is a different kernel -- pairwise or sequential -- and its reference has to mirror that order, not this one.

entries.title: An FP16 row normalized in FP32, including the reduction's return path
entries.surface: ub_to_reg_unpack and reg_to_ub_downsample around FP32 work on an FP16 register's even lanes; cast with RegLayout.ZERO both ways; cadd then reg_to_ub_single / ub_to_reg_single to broadcast lane 0; sqrt and div standing in for a missing rsqrt; muls / adds / mul / dup
study_for: The reduction's return path, which no other example here walks. `cadd` leaves the whole-register sum in lane 0 and nothing else; `reg_to_ub_single` parks that one lane in a UB cell and `ub_to_reg_single` brings it back across all 64. That round trip through memory is the mechanism -- there is no register-to-register broadcast of a single lane in this vocabulary, and a kernel that assumed one would be reading lane 0's value in lane 0 only.

FP16 data, FP32 arithmetic, and the even lanes are the seam between them. `ub_to_reg_unpack` puts 64 dense FP16 elements on the even lanes of an FP16 register; `cast` with `RegLayout.ZERO` widens exactly those into a 64-lane FP32 register; the result narrows back onto the even lanes and `reg_to_ub_downsample` compacts them. The cast policy in docs/api/formats.md owns why the layout selects those lanes and why the mask width matters.

No `rsqrt` exists here, so the scale is `sqrt` then `div` with a register of ones. That is two instructions and one extra rounding compared with a fused reciprocal square root -- and the comparison is still bitwise, which is the useful part: the reference mirrors the same operation order in FP64.

`eps` is observable in exactly one case, and the case matrix is built around that. `zero_row` sends an all-zero row through: with the bias it normalizes to a finite zero, without it the row divides by zero and arrives NaN. Everywhere else 2^-10 is far below one FP16 ulp of the result, so a matrix without that row cannot distinguish an implementation that applies eps from one that drops it.

Why bitwise rather than a tolerance. The kernel computes in FP32 and narrows once with ties-to-even; the reference computes in FP64 and narrows once. On these four cases they agree in every bit, so a one-ulp disagreement is a finding rather than noise -- and the failure output prints the ulp distance for exactly that reason.
do_not_copy_when: You were going to drop the epsilon because it never shows up. It shows up on an all-zero row, and an all-zero row is not exotic in a normalization -- a masked-out block produces one.

You expect bitwise agreement to survive a different case matrix. It holds for these inputs and this operation order. Widen the domain, reorder the reduction, or fuse the reciprocal square root, and the right answer is a stated tolerance, not this comparison.

You need more than one participant. This is `block_dim=1` and one vector participant owns every row. Splitting rows across cores is straightforward, but the reduction's UB cell is then per-core state and nothing here establishes that.

Your reduction is not over a whole register. `cadd` reduces all 64 lanes; a row shorter than the register needs a mask, and then lane 0 holds the sum of the lanes the mask admitted -- which is a different kernel with a different reference.

entries.title: Saturation flags read back, and three levels of state restored
entries.surface: get_saturation_flag("cast") / get_saturation_flag("float") and their setters; barrier(Pipe.ALL) around a mode-state change; a flag value used as a DMA slice index; a @vf body publishing a Var difference
study_for: The flag read is made observable instead of trusted. After setting `cast` true and `float` false, the kernel uses the values it reads back as the offset of its DMA source slice: `ub[0:1, (a * 8):(a * 8 + 8)]`. So the output is `x[8:16]` exactly when the read answered 1, and the comparison of the data output is therefore a comparison of the reads. A getter that returned a stale value changes which eight lanes arrive.

Three levels of state, unwound in order. The launch's own pair is captured first; the case's `initial_mode` pair is installed and captured; the kernel's working pair is set, used, and restored to the case's; the launch's pair is put back last. Four cases cover every initial combination, so the case where the kernel's value and the value it must restore differ (`initial_2`) is actually exercised rather than assumed to behave like the others.

`restored` is the restoration checked rather than claimed: the kernel XORs what it reads back against what it saved, ORs the two flags' differences together, and publishes the result through a `@vf` body. And the destination arrives holding 12345, not zero -- so a status that was never published fails, where a zero-filled destination would have let it pass silently. That choice is the whole reason the output is worth having.

`barrier(Pipe.ALL)` brackets every flag change. The flags are mode state shared by the pipes, not an operand of any instruction, so changing one while work is in flight would apply it to an unpredictable part of that work. The barriers are what make the three phases separable at all.
do_not_copy_when: You want to know what the saturation flags *do*. This unit checks reading them, writing them and restoring them -- not the arithmetic they control. The behaviour of a saturating cast is a separate example, and a green run here says nothing about it.

You are leaving the flags where your kernel left them. The sample this one replaced did exactly that, and it leaked its changed state into whatever ran next. If your kernel changes mode state, it owns restoring it, and this unit shows what the check for that looks like.

You are changing a flag inside a synchronised region without a barrier. The `auto_sync()` block here still brackets its flag writes with `barrier(Pipe.ALL)`, because the flags are not data and the dependency is not one autosync can see.

entries.title: Dynamic scalar absolute value at six native widths
entries.surface: api.scalar_abs on an api.Var, with Var.GetValueFrom / Var.SetValueTo moving one GM element at a time; six dtypes (i8, i16, i32, i64, f16, f32) from one kernel body
study_for: How a dynamic scalar reaches GM at all. `api.Var(0, dtype)` declares a register of the case's own width, `GetValueFrom(source[row:row+1, col:col+1])` reads one element into it, and `SetValueTo` writes one element back. Nothing here goes through the vector unit, and nothing is tiled: the 2x8 tile is sixteen separate scalar reads and sixteen separate stores, which is what makes the per-element dtype observable.

Why the result keeps the case's width. `api.Var(api.scalar_abs(value), dtype)` names the destination dtype explicitly instead of letting the expression's type decide, so the store is in i8 for the i8 case and in f16 for the f16 one. A body that computed the magnitude in a wider register and stored that would disagree with the reference in dtype, not just in value, and the comparison checks dtype before it checks bytes.

What a bitwise comparison buys here, and it is not pedantry. `abs` is exactly the operation that must turn -0.0 into +0.0. `torch.equal` reads those two as the same number, so a kernel that copied its source straight through would pass a value comparison on both float cases -- the f32 and f16 inputs each carry a +0.0 and a -0.0 -- and only a byte comparison catches it. The same comparison is what makes the infinities and the normal minimum mean something rather than being rounded into agreement.

Two widths where the C spelling itself is the risk. For i64 the backend has to reach the `long` overload of `::abs`; the `int` one would truncate, which is why this case carries values past 2^31. For f16 there is no native A5 scalar magnitude at all: the emitted expression is `(half)::abs((float)value)`, a widen and a narrow around the operation, and the endpoints in this case are what show that round trip preserved them.

Why the signed integer minimum is absent. Its magnitude is not representable in its own width, so there is no correct answer a reference could state. The unit's `check_domain` asserts it stays out of the inputs rather than leaving a reader to wonder whether the omission was an oversight -- an honest domain boundary, written down where the cases are.
do_not_copy_when: You want the magnitude of a whole tile. This is one scalar instruction per element -- sixteen of them for a 2x8 tile -- because the point is the dynamic scalar path. A tile of data belongs on the vector unit, where one instruction covers every lane.

Your dtype is BF16. `scalar_abs_expr` refuses it at the source line rather than approximating it: A5 has no target-supported BF16 scalar conversion for this (M10-055). A widening to FP32 around it is a different kernel, and it is not what this one would give you.

Your dtype is unsigned. The backend returns the value untouched for every `u*` width and for `b1`, which is correct and also means there is nothing to check: no case here covers one, and a passing run says nothing about that path.

You intend to pass the signed minimum. The operation has no representable answer for it and this unit's domain excludes it; a caller that needs one has to decide what it wants -- saturation, a widened result type, or a refusal -- before reusing any of this.

entries.title: Scalar control flow: a compile-time unroll beside a run-time loop
entries.surface: Var(0) with in-place addition; unroll(n) for a compile-time repetition; for index in range(scalar) for a run-time loop; if / else, break and continue inside it; Var.SetValueTo(GM slice); a kernel(mode="vec") entry taking an i32 argument
study_for: Which parts of the control flow are decided when. `unroll(3)` is three copies of the body at compile time; `range(n)` is a loop whose trip count arrives as a scalar argument; the `break`, the `continue` and the `if index > 4` are all run-time decisions inside it. One kernel, both kinds, nothing else in the way.

The five values of `n` are the boundaries, not samples. Zero iterations isolates the unroll's contribution. One iteration is skipped by `continue`, so the answer does not move. Four is before the `> 4` branch has ever been taken. Nine is exactly the break point. Twelve is past it -- and must give the same answer as nine.

That last equality is the whole content of the `break`, and no single case states it: main.py compares the two runs to each other and prints the verdict. A kernel that ignored the break would agree with the reference at n=9 and disagree only at n=12.
There is no vector arithmetic and no transfer here at all -- one scalar, one store of one integer. It is the smallest place to read how a `Var` behaves and how it reaches memory.
do_not_copy_when: Your loop bound is not bounded. The break at 9 is what keeps this kernel's cost fixed; a runtime loop with no ceiling is a different design question.
You expect `unroll` to take a runtime value. It is a compile-time repetition; the body is emitted that many times.
You want the vector unit. Nothing here touches it; this is scalar control flow and a single scalar store.

entries.title: Scalar helpers: arithmetic, bits, alignment and the worker queries
entries.surface: var_add / var_sub / var_mul / var_div / var_mod / var_and / var_or / var_xor / var_shl / var_shr / var_inv; Min, Max, CeilDiv; Align8 through Align256; GetVecNum, GetVecIdx, GetSubBlockIdx; scalar_sqrt, scalar_abs; api.unroll over a list of results
study_for: Twenty-eight helpers, one observed lane each. The results are collected into a Python list and stored with `api.unroll(24)`, so the kernel body stays one line per store while every helper gets its own comparable byte. The integer destination arrives filled with -999 and the float one with NaN, and `check_domain` refuses to run if either poison could be a legitimate answer -- which is what turns a missing store into a named failure rather than a wrong number.

The last integer lane is about shift semantics, not about shifting. `unsigned = Var(2**63 + 15, u64)` then `var_shr(unsigned, 63)` answers 1. Read the same bits as `i64` and the value is negative, where an arithmetic shift would answer -1. The lane exists so that the unsigned type is doing something observable rather than being a declaration nobody checks.

Two spellings of floating division must agree. `var_div(1.5, 2.0)` takes literals the frontend can fold; `var_div(numerator, denominator)` takes two runtime cells. Both lanes must read exactly 0.75, which is the cheap way to state that the helper is one operation with one rounding rather than a fast path and a slow path.

The worker queries are launch properties, made comparable. `GetVecNum`, `GetVecIdx` and `GetSubBlockIdx` answer 1, 0 and 0 for this one-participant launch, and they are stored like any other result -- so the reference states what the launch configuration is, instead of the kernel assuming it.

Why two values of `n` and not one. 37 is below 64 and 81 above it, so the six alignment helpers agree in different places in the two cases (40/48/64/64/128/256 against 88/96/96/128/128/256). One value alone would let a helper that used the wrong modulus still look correct.
do_not_copy_when: Your integers can be negative. The declared domain here is positive integers, and the division and modulo lanes are only checked for those. Signed quotient and remainder semantics -- which way each rounds -- are a separate question this unit does not answer.

You are targeting PyPTO Pro and need the float half. `scalar.sqrt` is refused there (A5-UP-002) and `scalar.abs` too (A5-UP-001). The integer bitwise and alignment operators are mapped, so the refusal is not about the first 24 lanes -- but a kernel that needs a scalar square root has no spelling on that backend today.

You are reading the worker queries as constants. They answer what this launch is: one vector participant, `block_dim=1`. A launch with more participants gives different values in different cores, and nothing here exercises that.

entries.title: Scalar cells: a UB load, a copy, and two first-element stores
entries.surface: Var(value, dtype) as a cell; Var.GetValueFrom / Var.SetValueTo and their <<= / >>= spellings; Var(other) copying a cell; one kernel source across the a2, a3, a5 and a5pr facades
study_for: The constructor value is a sentinel, not an initialisation you can rely on. `Var(-999.0, f32)` has to be replaced by the runtime load, and -999 appears nowhere in the reference -- `check_domain` asserts that. So a load that did not happen prints as -998 in column 3 and -999 in column 4 rather than as a small numerical difference, and the failure names itself.

Copying a `Var` makes another cell. `copied = api.Var(value)` then `value += 1.0`: column 3 gets the incremented original and column 4 the untouched copy, from the same source element. Those two lanes side by side are the whole statement about value semantics -- if the copy were a reference, both lanes would hold the incremented value and the kernel would still compile and run.

A store addresses only the first element of the view it is given. Every view here is narrowed to one column (`local[:, 3:4]`), which is not decoration: a wider view stores to its first element and leaves the rest alone, with no diagnostic, so the narrowing is what makes the intent checkable.

The two spellings must agree byte for byte. `GetValueFrom`/`SetValueTo` and `<<=`/`>>=` are the same two instructions, and the pair of cases shares one seed so that any difference between them is a defect rather than a different input. That is cheaper to maintain than a prose claim that they are equivalent.

One source, four facades. `make_scalar(device, spelling)` imports `ascriptor.<device>` and builds the identical body, so `--device a2` and `--device a5pr` run the same kernel text against different targets with the same reference. UB scalar access needs M10-016, and the PTO adapters this relies on were repaired by M10-061.
do_not_copy_when: You expect `Var(other)` to alias. It does not, and the two stored lanes here exist to show it. Code that relies on aliasing needs the same cell, not a copy of it.
You are handing a store a multi-element view on purpose. Only the first element is written. A range of lanes is a vector store, not a scalar one.

You need a dynamic scalar dtype conversion. Nothing here converts: one cell, one dtype, throughout. Explicit dynamic scalar dtype conversion remains a separate PyPTO Pro API gap, so a green run of this unit on that backend says nothing about it.

You are reading this as a vector example. The row is staged in UB and copied back wholesale; the only per-element work is scalar. A lane-wise computation belongs on the vector unit and looks nothing like this.

entries.title: Nine SIMT atomic families with order-independent answers
entries.surface: @simt(num_threads=256) bodies with simt_thread_id / simt_thread_num; simt_atomic_add / sub / max / min / exch / and / or / xor / cas on a GMTensor; allvec_ready / allvec_wait on Pipe.V; a kernel(mode="mix") launch with two vector participants
study_for: Order independence is a precondition, not a property of the word 'atomic'. Add, sub, max, min, and, or and xor commute, so their result is a function of the contributor multiset. `exch` does not commute -- it is only comparable here because every contributor writes the same value, its column index. `cas` does not either -- it is comparable because exactly one candidate can ever match: threads below the column count compare against `i`, which the row was seeded with, and all other threads compare against -7, which nothing is. Either order gives 1000 + i.

The seeding is a separate launch, and it has to be globally visible before any atomic runs. `seed_rows_simt` writes every row from the caller's `initial`; `allvec_ready(0, pipe=Pipe.V)` and `allvec_wait(0, pipe=Pipe.V)` are the all-vector rendezvous that makes those writes visible to the *other* participant. Without it the second participant's atomics could read a row before the first had seeded it, and nothing else in the kernel orders them.

Two participants, 256 threads each, and the index arithmetic says so. A thread's global id is `vec_idx * simt_thread_num() + simt_thread_id()`, and the seeding loop strides by `vec_num * simt_thread_num()`. Those two expressions are the whole difference between one participant and several -- copying a single-participant body and raising the launch's participant count leaves every thread doing the same work.

The initial rows are chosen so the seeding is observable: max starts at -1000000 and min at 1000000 so every contributor moves them, `and` starts at -1 (all bits) so it can only lose bits, and add and sub start at seed-dependent non-zero values. A kernel that dropped the seeding launch entirely would still produce plausible rows, and the `nonzero_initial_rows` case is what refuses them.
do_not_copy_when: Your atomic family is not order-independent in the way you are using it. An unsynchronised `exch` with differing values, or a `cas` with more than one matching candidate, has no single right answer -- and then a comparison against a reference is measuring luck.

You are reading `allvec_ready` / `allvec_wait` as a core-local barrier. It is a rendezvous across vector participants. A barrier inside one participant would not have made the seeding visible to the other.

You need this in a pure `vec` launch. The topology is `mode="mix"` with two participants; the thread geometry and the rendezvous both depend on that. A single-participant version is a different kernel with a simpler and less interesting synchronisation story.

entries.title: SIMT scalar math, two different roundings, and bit classification
entries.surface: simt_exp / exp2 / log / log2 / log1p / sin / cos / tanh / rsqrt; simt_rint and simt_round; simt_floor / ceil / trunc; simt_fmod, simt_fma; simt_isnan / isinf / isfinite / popc / mul_hi / ffs inside an @simt(num_threads=64) body
study_for: `simt_rint` and `simt_round` are different operations, and the reference has to say so twice. rint takes ties to even; round takes them away from zero. Torch's own `round` is ties-to-even, so the reference spells the second rule out as `copysign(floor(abs(v) + 0.5), v)` rather than reusing it -- and the `rounding_and_bits` case puts x*10 on -12.5, -0.5, 0.5, 11.5 and 12.5 so the two answers actually separate.

The tolerance surface is as small as the arithmetic requires. Nine transcendentals and `fmod` carry a budget with both an element bound and a relative-norm bound; the five roundings, the FMA and all six integer rows are byte comparisons. Widening the rule to the whole output would have hidden a wrong rounding mode behind a transcendental's allowance.

The FMA row is bitwise because its multiplier was chosen to make that legitimate: `simt_fma(v, 2.0, 1.0)` against a reference of `x * 2 + 1`. Two is a power of two, so the product is exact in FP32 and the fused and unfused forms cannot disagree. Pick any other multiplier and the row needs a tolerance -- and then it stops being a check on the FMA.

The integer rows carry their own boundary values: 0, -1, -2^31 and 2^31-1 lead the bit carrier. `popc` therefore sees both 0 and 32 set bits, `mul_hi` squares the widest magnitudes, and `ffs` sees the zero word, which it has to answer 0 for -- the reference states that as `(word & -word).bit_length()` over an unsigned view, so the two's-complement carrier is explicit.

The classification rows read a separate input. `specials` is the arithmetic input with a NaN and both infinities planted in its first three lanes, so `isnan`, `isinf` and `isfinite` have something to classify without putting a NaN through the transcendentals -- which would have made their budgets meaningless.
do_not_copy_when: You are treating rint and round as the same operation. They differ on every exact tie, which is where rounding bugs live.

You are copying the FMA row's bitwise comparison with a different multiplier. It only holds because 2.0 is exact; anything else needs a budget, and the comparison stops distinguishing a fused multiply-add from two instructions.
You need a transcendental to be bit-exact. None of the nine is, here or anywhere: they carry a budget because the scalar primitive and the host library round independently.

Your integer carrier is unsigned. `popc` and `ffs` are checked over a signed 32-bit two's-complement carrier, and `mul_hi` is the signed high product. The unsigned variants are different operations and no case here covers them.

entries.title: Wrapping SIMT increment and decrement over a fixed cycle
entries.surface: simt_atomic_inc(cell, limit) and simt_atomic_dec(cell, limit) with their wraparound; simt_threadfence(); two @simt(num_threads=256) launches in one vec kernel, one seeding and one contributing
study_for: `LIMIT` is the top of the cycle, not its length. `simt_atomic_inc(cell, 5)` counts 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 0 -- six values -- and the decrement wraps from 0 back to 5. So four contributors take the increment row from 0 to 4 and the decrement row from 5 to 1, and the reference states both as modular arithmetic over `LIMIT + 1`.

The reference counts contributors and models no thread order, which is the only honest reference for an atomic. It works here because both operations commute over the cycle: any interleaving of four increments from zero lands on four. An atomic whose result depended on the order would need either a lock or a different check.

The thread geometry is the whole input. 256 threads over 64 columns is four contributors each, and the `different_dummy` case exists to say so out loud: the dummy tensor is copied to UB to satisfy the input-tensor requirement and never read, so two different dummies must give identical output. That also means this example cannot catch a data-path defect -- it is not measuring one.

`simt_threadfence()` between the two atomics is a thread fence and is described as nothing more. It orders one thread's memory operations; it does not rendezvous threads and it is not a global barrier. The seeding is a separate launch precisely because a fence would not have been enough.
do_not_copy_when: You read `LIMIT` as a count. It is the inclusive top of the cycle, so the period is `LIMIT + 1`. Off by one here is off by one in every column.
You expect `simt_threadfence()` to synchronise threads. It does not. Ordering between threads needs the atomics themselves, a separate launch, or an all-vector rendezvous.

You want a counter whose final value tells you the contributor count. Over a cycle it tells you the count modulo `LIMIT + 1`. With more contributors than the cycle admits, several different counts give the same answer -- which is a property of a ring counter, not a defect, and is why this example's contributor count is smaller than its cycle.

entries.title: Score/ID records sorted and merged, with the tie handled honestly
entries.surface: sort32(dst, scores, ids, lists); mergesort4(dst, sorted_lists, per_list, stride); mergesort_2seq(dst, first, second, n0, n1) -- records as an FP32 score word beside a UINT32 ID word
study_for: How to check an operation whose output is not fully determined, without weakening the check. The order inside an equal-score group is the primitive's business, so `canonical_records` verifies everything that is determined first -- the scores descend, each ID appears exactly once, every ID is paired with its own score's bits -- and only then sorts tie groups by ID so the remaining comparison can be bitwise. Loosening the comparison instead would have given up the permutation property, which is the one most worth keeping.

The duplicate-ID check is independent of the scores, and that is the point of it. If a sort loses one record and repeats another, every gathered score can still tie and the output can still descend. Only the ID multiset notices. The `tied_scores` case is built so that this is the check doing the work.

IDs start at 1000 while positions run 0..127. So an implementation that returned each record's position instead of its ID fails immediately rather than passing on the cases where the two happen to coincide -- and `check_domain` asserts that separation rather than assuming the generator kept it.

A record is two 32-bit words, not a 64-bit value: the score's bits and the ID's bits side by side. The comparison is over those words, which is why the reference builds its expected output with `view(torch.int32)` rather than as floats -- a score of -0.0 and one of +0.0 would otherwise compare equal while occupying different bits.

Three primitives, one after another, on the same data: `sort32` produces four sorted lists, `mergesort4` merges all four, `mergesort_2seq` merges two of them. Each output is checked independently, so a merge that assumed its inputs were already globally ordered -- rather than per-list -- is visible in the merged lists and not in the sorted ones.
do_not_copy_when: You need a stable sort. Nothing here establishes one: the tie order is normalised away before the comparison, precisely because it is not guaranteed. If your algorithm depends on equal scores keeping their input order, that is a property you have to build and check yourself.

Your records are wider than two words. The score/ID pair is the layout these primitives take. A payload larger than an ID has to be gathered afterwards by the ID, which is a separate step and a separate example.
You are comparing scores as floats. Two zeros with different signs are equal as numbers and different as records. The comparison here is over words for that reason.

entries.title: A non-contiguous GM view, with its shape, strides and offset in elements
entries.surface: GM[...].flatten().view(shape, strides, offset=) as the source of a transfer into a contiguous UB tile; auto_sync() around the two moves; one kernel(mode="vec") launch
study_for: All three numbers are in *elements*, not bytes: the logical shape, the stride per axis, and the offset. `view([2, 16], [128, 2], offset=3)` reads 32 of the source's 256 elements, and the last one it touches is element 161 -- which `check_domain` computes from the declared numbers rather than taking on trust.

A non-unit innermost stride is supported for a read and is a gap for a write. That asymmetry is the reason the kernel loads through the view and stores a complete contiguous tile, rather than doing the interesting thing on both ends.

`check_domain` refuses a case where a contiguous read of the same length, or a read from element 0, would give the same answer. Without those two refusals the strides and the offset could both be wrong and the comparison would still pass.
The comparison is bitwise because nothing arithmetic happens: a strided read moves bits without touching them, so any difference is an address difference.
do_not_copy_when: You want to *write* through a non-unit innermost stride. That is a gap; this example reads through one and writes a contiguous tile.
