You are counting in bytes. Strides and the offset here are element counts, and a byte-based figure is wrong by the element size in every axis.
Your view can reach past its source. Nothing at run time clips it; the check that the last element read is inside the source is the example's own, and it belongs in any caller that computes strides.

entries.title: Packed rows walked through unaligned loads and counted stores
entries.surface: unalign_reg_for_load / unalign_reg_for_store state, ub_cursor, ub_to_reg_unalign_pre / ub_to_reg_unalign / reg_to_ub_unalign / reg_to_ub_unalign_post for the streaming path, and ub_to_reg_unalign_once / reg_to_ub_unalign_once for the stateless one
study_for: Two spellings of the same walk, and what separates them. The streaming path carries state: one `unalign_reg_for_load` and one `unalign_reg_for_store`, a `ub_cursor` per row, a prime before the row's first chunk and a `reg_to_ub_unalign_post` that closes the row's store chain. The stateless path carries none: each chunk names its own element offset and nothing is remembered between them. Both are run over all six geometries, and both must produce the same bytes.

The source allocation is deliberately larger than the payload. `capacity = ((cells + 64 + 7) // 8) * 8` adds a full register of slack past the data and rounds the end up, which is what makes a full-register load legal when the last chunk of a row is partial. The destination has no slack at all -- it is exactly `cells` -- so every store passes an explicit `count` that has to stay inside the row. Read those two allocations together; copying one without the other is how this kind of walk goes wrong.

Only row 0 is necessarily aligned. With no padding between rows, row `i` starts at element `i * width`, so the byte phase of a row depends on the width: the 3x64 geometry has every row aligned (the control), while 5x17 and 4x33 put almost every row at a different phase. Having both in the matrix is what makes a pass mean something -- an implementation that only handled the aligned case would fail eleven of the twelve cases rather than looking fine.

The body adds the row index and nothing else. That is a diagnostic decision: every cell of row `i` differs from the input by exactly `i`, so a cell that came from the wrong row is off by the difference of two row numbers, and the failure output prints those offsets. A body that computed something interesting would make the same addressing mistake much harder to read.
do_not_copy_when: You are about to give the destination the source's slack, or the source the destination's exactness. The asymmetry is the point: reads may overrun into slack, writes may not overrun at all.

You are treating a green model run as proof that the final store-chain flush is optional. It is not. `reg_to_ub_unalign_post` closes the chain, and a CPU check cannot establish the vendor hardware's buffering behaviour when it is left out -- that question needs a card.

You are reusing the streaming state across rows. The cursor and the load state are primed per row here. Carrying either into the next row leaves the previous row's phase in it, and nothing in the API stops you.

Your rows are padded to a register boundary. Then none of this is needed -- an ordinary aligned load and store per row is both simpler and faster, and the geometry that proves it is `3x64`, the one case here where the unaligned path has nothing to correct.

entries.title: Sixty-four-bit signed and unsigned register arithmetic, and per-lane variable shifts
entries.surface: Reg(DT.int64) and Reg(DT.uint64) with add / sub / mul / and / or / xor / not, fixed and register-valued shifts, dup of a 64-bit literal, cmpsel against a register and against a scalar, abssub and fused square-plus-b; the extended element-wise set plus the cadd / cmax / cmin row reductions; a second register supplying a per-lane shift count at 32 and 64 bits
study_for: Forty-four named outputs, one per operation per family, so an operation that was never emitted fails as itself. Four families share the folder because they share one register width, not one instruction set: `native` and `extended` are signed, `unsigned` is the same core over UINT64, and `shifts` takes its count from a register rather than a literal.

The unsigned family is why the signed one is not enough, and the difference is checkable rather than notional. `select_reg` picks by `x > y`: unsigned and signed comparison disagree on exactly the pairs whose high bits differ. `shift_right` is logical for UINT64 and arithmetic for INT64. `check_domain` counts the disagreeing lane pairs and requires at least one high-bit lane, so a case that could not distinguish the two is refused instead of passing.

`cadd`, `cmax` and `cmin` are row reductions: the kernel writes a full row and only the first lane is defined. main.py slices that lane and compares it, and `check_domain` asserts the reference's shape is one column -- publishing the whole row would compare undefined lanes and publishing none would compare nothing.

The reference is Python's unbounded integers, wrapped only where the carrier wraps: `% 2**64` for the unsigned family, `signed(x << s, bits)` for a left shift. That is the whole reason the comparison can be bitwise. A floating comparison of 64-bit integers would excuse precisely the lost low bits this example exists to detect, and there is no tolerance anywhere in it.

The signed inputs stay inside a no-overflow domain -- 2**29 for the native family, 2**47 for the extended one -- because `mul` and `square_plus_b` square them. The unsigned lanes have no such limit: they wrap, and the reference says so with an explicit modulo. Two families, two different reasons the answer is defined.

The dup outputs carry 64-bit literals that do not fit 32 bits: `2**40 + 12345` signed and `2**63 + 2**40 + 7` unsigned. `check_domain` asserts both in every lane, which is what catches a literal truncated on the way into the instruction.
do_not_copy_when: Your signed operands can overflow. The domain is bounded so the products are exact; past it the answer is whatever the carrier does, and nothing here establishes that. The unsigned family is the one that wraps, deliberately.
Your shift count is not in 0..30. The per-lane counts are checked into that range; a count at or past the width is not covered, and neither is a negative one.
You are reading a reduction's full output row. Only the first lane is defined; the rest is whatever the kernel left there.

You expect signed and unsigned to differ only in how you print them. They differ in ordering and in shift-right, which is the substance of this example -- two of the forty-four outputs exist only to show it.

Your row is not 32 complete lanes, or you want more than one vector participant. Every family declares complete rows and one participant; a partial row would need its own statement about the undefined lanes.
